     3.1.   The   respondent,      National   Building   Construction

     Corporation Limited (hereinafter referred to as “NBCC”) was

     New Bombay (now Navi Mumbai), for an agreed contractual

6.   We have heard learned counsel appearing on behalf of the

     parties and perused the record. The question that falls for our

     determination is whether Clause 26 of the SCC operates as a

     contractual bar within the meaning of Section 31(7)(a) of the

     1996 Act barring the Arbitral Tribunal from awarding pre-

     reference and pendente lite interest on the substantive claims

     allowed in favour of the appellant.


7.   For convenience, it is apposite to examine Clause 26 of the

     SCC, which reads as follows:

            “26. The sub-contractor shall be paid monthly running bill for the quantity
       already executed upto the end of previous month subject to the approval of
       quantity measured unless otherwise specified. The amount so payable in the
       estimated value of works shall be paid upto date, less the amount already paid.
       If the monthly interim payment which become payable is not paid due to any
       reason, then 75% of the works executed and measured shall be paid to the sub-
       contractor as advance on written request. The payment to the sub-contractor will
       be released within seven days of NBCC receiving its payment from the clients
       i.e. CIDCO/IRCON.

           No claim for interest will be entertained by the corporation in respect of any
       balance payments or any deposit which may be held up with the corporation
       due to any dispute between the Corporation and sub-contractor or in respect of
       any delay on the part of the corporation in making monthly or final payments or
       otherwise.”

                                                                    Emphasis supplied.


8.   Section 31(7) of the 1996 Act provides for the statutory

     mechanism governing the award of interest in arbitral

     proceedings, which is reproduced hereunder:


                                                                                            13
          “31. Form and contents of arbitral award.—

           … (7) (a) Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, where and in so far as an
       arbitral award is for the payment of money, the arbitral tribunal may include in
       the sum for which the award is made interest, at such rate as it deems
       reasonable, on the whole or any part of the money, for the whole or any part of
       the period between the date on which the cause of action arose and the date on
       which the award is made.

           (b) A sum directed to be paid by an arbitral award shall, unless the award
       otherwise directs, carry interest at the rate of two per cent. higher than the
       current rate of interest prevalent on the date of award, from the date of award
       to the date of payment.

           Explanation.—The expression ‘current rate of interest’ shall have the same
       meaning as assigned to it under clause (b) of section 2 of the Interest Act, 1978
       (14 of 1978).”


9.   Upon perusal of Section 31(7)(a) of the 1996 Act, it is clear

     that the power of an Arbitral Tribunal to award interest for

     the pre-award period, i.e., from the date on which the cause

     of action arose up to the date on which the award is made

     (including both pre-reference and pendente lite periods), is

     expressly subject to the opening words - “Unless otherwise

     agreed by the parties”. Section 31(7) of the 1996 Act has to

     be construed harmoniously with Section 28(3) of the 1996

     Act, which provides for the Arbitral Tribunal to decide in

     accordance with the contractual terms governing the parties.


10. The principles governing contractual prohibitions on interest

     under Section 31(7)(a) of the 1996 Act have been recently

     considered by this Court in Larsen & Toubro Limited

     (supra), wherein this Court examined Clause 16(3) read with

     Clause 64(5) of the General Conditions of Contract. Clause

                                                                                           14
         16(3) expressly prohibited interest on “earnest money and

         security deposits or amounts payable to the Contractor under

         the Contract”, reinforced by Clause 64(5) which provided that

         “where the arbitral award is for the payment of money, no

         interest shall be payable on whole or any part of the money for

         any period till the date on which the award is made”.

         Reaffirming the law laid down in Sayeed Ahmed (supra),

         Sree Kamatchi Amman Constructions v. Divisional

         Railway Manager (Works),8 Bright Power Projects (supra)

         and Manraj Enterprises (supra), this Court in Larsen &

         Toubro Limited (supra) held that:

                “35. On perusal of Section 28(3) and Section 31(7)(a) of the Act, it is clear
            that the statutory scheme itself subordinates the discretion of the arbitrator to
            the contractual provisions governing interest.

                …

                43. Now, at this stage, it is pertinent to observe that this Court, thereafter,
            in the case of Manraj Enterprises (supra) had an occasion to consider similar
            issues involved in the present matter and had considered all the aforementioned
            decisions, including the decisions rendered in the cases of Bright Power Projects
            (India) (P) Ltd. (supra), Raveechee and Company (supra) and Ambica
            Construction vs. Union of India, (2017) 14 SCC 323 (a three-judge bench
            judgment of this Court). After considering the aforesaid decisions as well as
            several other decisions referred on the issue, this Court has observed in para 8
            and 11 as under: …

                    “11. In the said decision in Bright Power Projects [Union of India v.
                Bright Power Projects (India) (P) Ltd., (2015) 9 SCC 695 : (2015) 4 SCC
                (Civ) 702] , this Court also considered Section 31(7)(a) of the 1996 Act. It
                is specifically observed and held that Section 31(7) of the 1996 Act, by
                using the words “unless otherwise agreed by the parties” categorically
                specifies that the arbitrator is bound by the terms of the contract insofar
                as award of interest from the date of cause of action to date of the award
                is concerned. It is further observed and held that where the parties had
                agreed that no interest shall be payable, the Arbitral Tribunal cannot

           45. The provisions of the Act of 1996, including provisions contained in
       Section 31(7)(a) give paramount importance to the contract entered into between
       the parties and categorically restrict the power of an arbitrator to award pre-
       award/pendente lite interest when the parties have themselves agreed to the

       Clause 64(5) of GCC.”

11. It is contended on behalf of the appellant that the concluding

     phrase “or otherwise” of Clause 26 of the SCC must be

     interpreted applying the principles of ejusdem generis and

     noscitur a sociis to take colour from the preceding expressions

     concerning delay in releasing monthly or final payments and

     the expression “or otherwise” is restricted to withholding

     interest on delayed interim bills and cannot operate as an

     absolute bar against the grant of interest on substantive

     claims allowed by the Arbitral Tribunal.


12. However, we are unable to agree with the said contention. The

     doctrine of ejusdem generis becomes applicable only where

                                                                                         16
    the preceding terms of the general phrase follow a specific

    class forming a genus, thereby imparting the specific

    character to the subsequent general phrase. At this stage, it

    is relevant to note that where the provisions in a contract are

    disjunctively joined by the word “or”, every such phrase has

    to be examined independently due to its wide amplitude. The

    same issue was considered in Manraj Enterprises (supra)

    and subsequently reiterated in paragraphs 38 and 39 of

    Larsen & Toubro Limited (supra):

           “38. This Court in the decision rendered in the case of Manraj Enterprises
       (supra) has considered a similar submission canvassed on behalf of the party
       concerned and thereafter observed and held in para 12.1 as under:

              “12.1. It is required to be noted that Clause 16(1) is with respect to
          earnest money/security deposit. However, Clause 16(2) is specifically
          with respect to interest payable upon the earnest money or the security
          deposit or amounts payable to the contractor under the contract. The
          words used in Clause 16(2) is “or”. Therefore, the expression “amounts
          payable to the contractor under the contract” cannot be read in
          conjunction with “earnest money deposit” or “security deposit” by
          applying the principle of ejusdem generis. The expression “amounts
          payable to the contractor under the contract” has to be read
          independently and disjunctively to earnest money deposit and security
          deposit as the word used is “or” and not “and” between “earnest money
          deposit”, “security deposit” and “amounts payable to the contractor
          under the contract”. Therefore, the principle of ejusdem generis is not
          applicable in the present case.”

           39. Thus, it can be said that the rule of ejusdem generis is a tool of
       interpretation and is applicable only where the general words follow a specific
       class forming a genus. The expression “amounts payable to the contractor under
       the contract” used in Clause 16(3) is independent, distinct and of wide
       amplitude, and cannot be read down to defeat its plain meaning. Thus, the
       submission canvassed by the learned counsel for the respondent cannot be
       accepted.”

                                                                   Emphasis supplied.


13. Applying these principles to Clause 26 of the SCC in the

    present case, the Clause enumerates the following separate

                                                                                         17
         and distinct events disjunctively joined by the conjunction

         “or”:


         (i) any balance payments or any deposits - which may be held
         up with the corporation due to any dispute arising between
         the Corporation and the sub-contractor, OR
         (ii) in respect of any delay on the part of the corporation in
         making monthly or final payments, OR
         (iii) otherwise.


14. On careful consideration, it can be inferred that the preceding

         terms of the phrase “or otherwise” do not constitute a single,

         narrow genus restricted to delayed running payments and

         also include balance payments, withheld deposits and

         amounts withheld due to disputes. Consequently, the

         expression “or otherwise” is residuary in nature and has been

         consciously incorporated with wide amplitude to encompass

         every other conceivable circumstance under which a claim for

         interest might be asserted against the Corporation. In

         Lilavati Bai v. State of Bombay,9 the Constitution Bench

         of this Court held that the words “or otherwise” cannot be

         restricted by reference to the preceding expressions and were

         held to be words of extension and not limitation. Thus,


9
    (1957) 1 SCC 411.



                                                                     18
    restricting the scope of the expression “or otherwise” to only

    delays in monthly or final payments would render the term

    redundant and would amount to rewriting the contract

    entered into between the parties.


15. The reliance placed by the appellant upon Oil and Natural

    Gas Corporation Ltd. (supra) is also misplaced. In the said

    decision, the contractual clause was narrowly worded as “no

    interest shall be payable by ONGC on any delayed payment /

    disputed claim”, and did not incorporate any residuary

    expression and thus, this Court observed that a stipulation

    merely restricting interest on delayed payments cannot be

    construed as an absolute bar on pendente lite interest.

    However, in the said case, this Court itself recognized that

    where the contract prohibits granting pendente lite interest

    either expressly or by necessary implication as in the case of

    Sayeed    Ahmed    (supra)   and    Jaiprakash    Associates

    Limited (supra), the power of the arbitral tribunal to grant

    pendente lite interest stands excluded.


16. In contrast, in the present case, Clause 26 of the SCC

    concludes with the residuary phrase “or otherwise”. In

    Sayeed Ahmed (supra), the clause provided “G1.09. No claim

                                                                19
     for interest or damages will be entertained by the Government

     with respect to any money or balance which may be lying with

     the Government or any become due owing to any dispute,

     difference or misunderstanding between the Engineer-in-

     Charge on the one hand and the contractor on the other hand

     or with respect to any delay on the part of the Engineer-in-

     Charge in making periodical or final payment or any other

     respect whatsoever.” A similar clause was in question in the

     decision     of    Jaiprakash    Associates      Limited   (supra).

     Therefore,        the   High   Court   rightly    concluded   that

     incorporating the residuary term “or otherwise” stands on

     identical footing with the terminology “or any other respect

     whatsoever” interpreted in Sayeed Ahmed (supra) and

     Jaiprakash Associates Limited (supra), thereby operating

     as a contractual prohibition against granting pre-reference as

     well as pendente lite interest.


17. At this stage, it is also imperative to observe the distinction

     between pre-award interest under Section 31(7)(a) and post-

     award interest under Section 31(7)(b) of the 1996 Act, i.e.,

     Section 31(7)(a) is expressly subject to the contract between

     the parties whereas, Section 31(7)(b) provides for grant of


                                                                      20
     post-award interest unless the arbitral tribunal orders

     otherwise. This Court in Larsen & Toubro Limited (supra)

     observed as under:

           “47. With regard to the post-award interest, Section 31(7)(b) of the Act
       provides that unless the award otherwise directs, the sum awarded shall carry
       interest from the date of the award till payment. The legislative intent underlying
       this provision is twofold: first, to compensate the successful party for delayed
       realization of the award, and second, to ensure prompt compliance with the
       award by the judgment-debtor.
           48. Recently, this Court in the case of R.P. Garg (supra), has observed and
       held in para 9, 11 and 12 as under:

               “... 11. So far as the entitlement of the post-award interest is
          concerned, sub-Section (b) of Section 31(7) provides that the sum directed
          to be paid by the Arbitral Tribunal shall carry interest. The rate of interest
          can be provided by the Arbitrator and in default the statutory
          prescription will apply. Clause (b) of Section 31(7) is therefore in contrast
          with clause (a) and is not subject to party autonomy. In other words,
          clause (b) does not give the parties the right to “contract out” interest for
          the post-award period. The expression ‘unless the award otherwise
          directs’ in Section 31(7)(b) relates to rate of interest and not entitlement
          of interest. The only distinction made by Section 31(7)(b) is that the rate
          of interest granted under the Award is to be given precedence over the
          statutorily prescribed rate. The assumption of the High Court that
          payment of the interest for the post award period is subject to the
          contract is a clear error. …”

                                                                  Emphasis supplied.


     Therefore, the High Court rightly recognized this statutory

     distinction and restricted its interference to setting aside the

     pre-reference and pendente lite interest, while maintaining

     the award of post-award interest in favour of the appellant.


18. In light of the aforesaid analysis and discussion, the learned

     Arbitrator, being a creature of the contract, acted beyond his

     jurisdiction in granting pre-reference and pendente lite

     interest in contravention of Clause 26 of the SCC, which



                                                                                             21
     attracts Section 31(7)(a) of the 1996 Act. Thus, the High Court

     rightly acted under Sections 34 and 37 of the 1996 Act in

     setting aside the arbitral award dated 28.07.2016 to that

     limited extent, while maintaining the substantive claims of

     the appellant and post-award interest in favour of the

     appellant. Therefore, we find no error in the impugned

     judgment dated 20.03.2026 passed by the Division Bench of

     the High Court of Delhi in FAO(OS) (COMM) No. 18 of 2026,

     affirming the judgment of the learned Single Judge dated

     19.11.2025 in O.M.P. (COMM) No. 215 of 2022.


19. Accordingly, the present appeal is dismissed.

31. The attempt to reopen the validity of that assignment

    issue, forming a necessary ingredient in a cause of

    the same issue is relevant, one of the parties seeks to
    reopen that issue. Three elements in that regard must
    be satisfied i.e. identity of issue, finality of the earlier

    their privies; each of which is satisfied here. The
    doctrine rests upon finality, consistency and judicial
    discipline, and once a finding has attained finality

    subsequent proceedings arise under a different
    statute or seek a different relief. To permit the
    Appellants to reopen a concluded legal issue in the
    present proceedings would tantamount to a collateral
    attack    upon     binding   determinations    that    have
    attained finality up to this Court.

    corporate debtors, so that the value of a stressed
    enterprise is preserved rather than allowed to erode
    through delay. Speed is not an incidental virtue of the
    Code,     it   is    its   central   design   principle.   The
    architecture of Section 7, including the fourteen-day
    period for ascertaining default under sub-section (4),
    is built around the elimination of exactly the kind of
    delay that was the characteristic of the antecedent
    regime.

36. The means by which the Code secures that expedition
    must next be noticed, for the legislature did not treat
    every creditor alike in prescribing what must be
    shown before the process is set in motion. The
    distinction         between    financial   and    operational
    creditors under the Code is instructive in this regard.
    Financial contracts generally involve large sums and
    specified repayment schedules, defaults entitling the

    operational contracts carry no such stipulation and
    are recurring in nature. Financial debts owed to
    banks and financial institutions are, by their very
    nature, well-documented, and a default committed in
    respect     of     them   is   readily   verifiable.   That
    characteristic is the evidentiary premise upon which
    the trigger mechanism for financial creditors rests,
    and it explains why the Code dispenses, in their case,
    with the notice-and-dispute machinery prescribed by
    Sections 8 and 9 of the Code for operational creditors.
    The same asymmetry is carried into the statutory
    obligations of the two classes: Section 215(2) of the
    Code requires that a financial creditor shall submit
    financial information and information relating to
    assets over which a security interest has been
    created, whereas Section 215(3) of the Code provides
    only that an operational creditor may do so.

37. The Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee (BLRC)
    report explained the rationale in terms leaving no
    room for doubt. Since financial creditors have
    electronic records of their liabilities filed with the
    Information Utilities, an incontrovertible event of
    default upon any financial credit contract is readily
    verifiable by accessing that system, whereas the

    evidence available to an operational creditor may be

    importance emerge, first, that an Information Utility
    record was conceived as the primary and readily
    verifiable evidence of a financial creditor's default and
    second, that other means of proof were expressly
    contemplated in the meanwhile. The Code was thus
    designed from the outset with a hierarchy of proof in
    contemplation, an Information Utility record at the
    apex     and       other     documentary      material   in   the
    alternative.

38. The object of establishing Information Utilities was
    that considerable time was previously lost before all
    parties obtained the relevant information, that
    disputes upon such facts could consume years in
    court, and that it accordingly envisaged a competitive
    industry of information utilities holding an array of
    information about all firms at all times, so that upon
    commencement of the resolution process undisputed
    and complete information would become available to
    all persons involved within less than a day. An
    interpretation of Section 7 requiring the Adjudicating

    Authority to reconcile every contested ledger entry
    before recording its satisfaction would defeat that

    is incomplete. It further held that the Adjudicating

    information utility or other evidence produced by the
    financial creditor to satisfy itself that a default has
    occurred, and that it is of no matter that the debt is
    disputed so long as the debt is due.

40. Against the backdrop of the legal position enunciated

41. The definition is deliberately undemanding. It neither
    requires that the entire debt be due, nor that the full

    quantum be free of dispute, but only that some part
    of what is due and payable has not been paid. The
    words "whole or any part or instalment" are not
    inessential, they are the operative words of the
    definition, and they establish that the statutory
    conception of default is satisfied by a shortfall,
    however partial.

42. It follows that a fundamental distinction must be
    maintained         between    two      matters   which         the
    Appellants' submissions persistently conflate. The
    occurrence of default is a historical and static event
    which crystallises upon the date a debt became due
    and was not paid. The quantum of debt outstanding,
    by contrast, is dynamic, fluctuating upon account of
    accruing       interest,     default     interest,      charges,
    adjustments and part-repayments. The two enquiries
    are different in kind, and Section 7 is concerned with
    the first i.e. the occurrence of default.

43. Section 7(4) of the Code requires the Adjudicating
    Authority to ascertain the existence of a default within
    fourteen days of receipt of the application. That
    timeline is unintelligible if "ascertainment" is read to
    mean a full reconciliation of every contested ledger
    entry, every interest-rate reset and every rupee of
    appropriation across separate facilities spanning

    several years. The fourteen day window is the period
    allotted for a summary determination of a historical
    fact, and the legislature in prescribing this time has
    itself implicitly indicated the nature of the enquiry it
    contemplates.      For   the   purposes      of    Section      7,
    therefore, the Adjudicating Authority is concerned
    only with the existence of a financial debt and the
    occurrence of default. It is not required to determine,
    to the last rupee, the exact outstanding liability, as a
    civil court would in a suit for recovery of money.

44. The standard applicable at the admission stage is one
    of     preponderance      of   probabilities       upon       the
    documentary        material    placed   on        record.    The
    threshold is deliberately modest which is a summary,
    prima facie finding of financial debt and default,
    grounded in documentary evidence, rather than a full
    trial upon disputed facts. It is the substance of
    default, not the technical formality of proof, that must
    govern proceedings under Section 7. Where the
    records of an Information Utility by themselves, or the
    loan    documents,       account   statements,          balance
    confirmations, acknowledgements of liability, one-
    time settlement proposals and contemporaneous
    correspondence taken collectively, demonstrate that a
    sum exceeding the statutory threshold had become

    due and remained unpaid, the Adjudicating Authority
    is not expected to defer admission merely because the
    parties dispute the computation of interest, penal
    charges or other accounting entries. Such disputes
    may bear upon the ultimate quantification of the
    claim but they do not negate the occurrence of
    default.

45. The conclusion that the Adjudicating Authority under
    the Section 7 proceedings is not required to adjudicate
    upon the exact quantum of debt due from a corporate

    administrative and not quasi-judicial in character, his
    determinations being subject throughout to the
    oversight of the Adjudicating Authority. That is
    precisely the point. The Code establishes a two-stage
    process i.e. a summary determination of default at the
    threshold, and a detailed verification of quantum
    thereafter, with judicial supervision available at the
    second     stage. Were the Adjudicating Authority
    required at admission to determine conclusively the
    precise outstanding liability, the functions entrusted
    to the Resolution Professional under Section 18 of the
    code and IBBI(CIRP) Regulations would be rendered
    otiose. A construction producing that result cannot be
    correct. The trigger for initiation of the CIRP is the
    occurrence of a default, not the final adjudication of
    the creditor's entire claim.

47. Question I as framed in paragraph 34 above is
    answered accordingly in terms that the evidentiary

    and 7 has occurred is a summary, prima facie

    of probabilities from the documentary material placed
    on record. It requires a proof of the occurrence of

    default, a static historical event, and not the

    negate default and do not arrest admission as long as
    the statutory threshold requirement under Section 4
    of the Code is satisfied.

48. Since Section 7 of the Code does not contemplate a
    forensic reconstruction of accounts, the Code and the
    Regulations        promulgated         thereunder         furnish
    guidance upon what documentary material the
    Adjudicating Authority may treat as sufficient. That
    guidance yields a hierarchy.

49. Section 7(3)(a) of the Code requires the financial
    creditor to furnish, with the Section 7 application,
    "record of the default recorded with the information
    utility or such other record or evidence of default as
    may be specified". Section 7(4) of the Code provides:

          "(4) The Adjudicating Authority shall, within fourteen
          days of the receipt of the application under sub-
          section (2), ascertain the existence of a default from
          the records of an information utility or on the basis of
          other evidence furnished by the financial creditor
          under sub-section (3)."

50. Section 7(3)(a) places the record of default with the
    Information Utility first among the materials the
    financial creditor may furnish, and Section 7(4)
    directs ascertainment "from the records of an

    information utility", and only in the alternative,
    signalled by the disjunctive "or", upon the basis of
    other evidence. The Information Utility record is thus,
    by statutory design, a self-sufficient basis for the
    Adjudicating Authority's ascertainment. It is not one
    item among many in an undifferentiated evidentiary
    mass.

51. The operational procedure underlying an information
    utility record as provided in the IBBI (Information
    Utility) regulations deserves statement, since it
    explains the weight an authenticated record carries.
    A creditor submitting information of default must
    furnish proof of the debt and proof of the default, so
    that what is placed before the Information Utility is
    not a bare assertion but a documented filing
    supported at the threshold by the underlying record.
    The Information Utility then delivers that information
    to the debtor, seeking confirmation within the
    specified time, and upon his failure to respond issues
    three reminders, allowing seven days in each
    instance. Only two consequences follow. Where the
    debtor confirms the information of default, or does not
    respond even after three reminders, the status
    recorded is that of authenticated and a Record of
    Default is issued. Where the debtor disputes it, the

    status recorded is that of disputed and what is issued
    is an Information of Dispute. The mechanism is
    disciplined        at    both   ends:    the      creditor    must
    substantiate the default when he files it, and the
    debtor is notified, reminded three times over, and
    invited to give reasons and evidence before a Record
    of Default is issued. It thus gives such records a
    reliability    exceeding        that    of   ordinary        private
    documents, because it embeds within the record itself
    the    debtor's         own   opportunity,     and    failure,    to
    contradict it.

52. The legal weight that ought to be given to an
    authenticated           information     utility    record     finds
    reinforcement in the general law of evidence. The
    process of authentication functions, in substance, as
    an admission of the debt and the default as between
    the parties to it. A debtor who does not dispute a
    default recorded against it within the authentication
    window has, by its conduct, permitted the creditor
    and the other stakeholders in the process to treat that
    default as accepted. Section 31 of the Indian Evidence
    Act, 1872 (hereinafter, “IEA”) or Section 25 of the
    Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (hereinafter,
    “BSA”) clarifies that such an admission is not by itself
    conclusive proof of the matter admitted, but expressly

    provides that an admission may operate as an
    estoppel under the provisions that follow. Section 115
    of the IEA or Section 121 of the BSA embodies exactly
    that estoppel, precluding a party who by its
    declaration, act or omission has intentionally caused
    or permitted another to believe a thing to be true and
    to act upon that belief from afterwards denying its
    truth.

53. A corporate debtor which allows an Information Utility
    record to go unchallenged through the authentication
    process, thereby causing the Adjudicating Authority
    and the financial creditor to proceed upon the footing
    that default is undisputed, cannot subsequently be
    heard to deny the fact of that default in the Section 7
    proceedings itself. The "not conclusive" language of
    Section 31 of the IEA and the estoppel under Section
    115 of the IEA are not in conflict but they answer two
    different questions. Section 31 of the IEA clarifies that
    an authenticated record is not, as a matter of general
    evidentiary theory incapable of being contradicted by
    any evidence whatsoever. Section 115 tells us that a
    particular     debtor,   in   those   circumstances,     is
    precluded from being the party to contradict it.

54. The evidentiary burden upon a corporate debtor
    seeking to rebut a record of default issued upon

    authenticated status is accordingly substantially
    higher than the ordinary threshold of a mere plausible
    dispute or a bare preponderance arising from self-
    serving assertions. To permit easy rebuttal of such
    documentary evidence through bald denials would
    defeat the legislative intent underlying Chapter V of
    Part IV of the Code relating to information utilities
    and would return the law to the very condition of
    years-long factual controversy regarding the existence
    of default in the first place which the BLRC identified
    as the principal source of delay in insolvency
    resolution proceedings.

55. It can accordingly be said that an authenticated
    Information Utility record, that is to say a Record of
    Default, does not become irrebuttable or legally
    conclusive proof of default in the abstract, but it
    creates a presumption of very high evidentiary value,
    displaceable only by clear, cogent, credible and
    compelling material, and not by bare denial, by
    bookkeeping        disagreement,   or   by    a     claim
    unsupported by any material whatsoever. In the
    absence of material displacing such presumption, the
    Record of default, standing alone is sufficient to prima
    facie establish the occurrence of default for the
    purposes of Section 7.

    is for this reason that the legislature has adopted
    "default" under Section 3(12), and not commercial or
    balance-sheet insolvency as the jurisdictional trigger.

    await the corporate debtor's irreversible financial

    its preventive and remedial architecture and defeat its

69. Neither explanation creates new law. Both are
    introduced by the familiar language of clarification
    and removal of doubt, and neither alters the pre-
    existing position, each makes explicit only what was
    already implicit in the Code. The sufficiency of an
    Information Utility record was already carried by
    Section 7(4) and by the design of the Code. The
    hierarchy set out in answer to the second question of
    law framed in paragraph 34 above is thus placed
    beyond cavil by express legislative enactment, and the
    reasoning of this Court would have been identical had
    the amendment not been effectuated.

70. A word is due upon the Information Utility mechanism
    itself. It is an innovation of Indian origin, without any
    direct parallel in comparable insolvency regimes at
    the time of its introduction. A regulated repository of
    financial information, authenticated through the
    debtor's own participation or acquiescence, designed
    so that the fact of default may be ascertained at the
    threshold without recourse to a protracted enquiry.
    Almost ten years have now passed since the Code
    came into force. The framework has matured,


 C.A. No. 12195/2025                             Page 45 of 50
    financial creditors submit the information of default
    as a matter of routine, and the corporate debtors can
    no longer claim unfamiliarity either with the process
    of authentication or with the consequences of silence.
    The      Bankruptcy   Law     Reforms     Committee's
    observation that until Information Utilities became
    ubiquitous financial creditors might establish default
    in the manner available to operational creditors was
    addressed to a period of transition and that period has
    long passed. It is accordingly imperative that the
    Adjudicating Authorities accord the weight which the
    Code, and now Explanation II to the amended Section
    7(5), assign to it.

71. It is convenient to summarise the conclusions
    reached:

    (i) The jurisdiction of this Court under Section 62 of
    the Code is confined to questions of law arising out of
    the order of the Appellate Tribunal. Where the
    Adjudicating Authority and the Appellate Tribunal
    have concurrently returned findings of fact and law
    upon the same material, those findings are not to be
    disturbed unless shown to be perverse, based upon
    no evidence, arrived at by ignoring material evidence,
    or founded upon an erroneous legal standard.




 C.A. No. 12195/2025                           Page 46 of 50
   (ii) The status of the Respondent no.1 as a financial
   creditor within the meaning of Section 5(7) of the Code
   stands conclusively established by the Assignment
   Agreement dated 27.12.2022, the validity of which
   has been upheld by the High Court of Karnataka and
   affirmed by this Court. The challenge to the
   assignment is barred by the principles of issue
   estoppel.

   (iii) Section 7 of the Code establishes a summary
   jurisdiction.      The   evidentiary   threshold       for
   ascertaining default is that of preponderance of
   probabilities upon the documentary material placed
   on record, and not        a forensic reconciliation of
   accounts. The occurrence of a default is a static
   historical event whereas the quantum of a debt
   outstanding is dynamic. The role of the Adjudicating
   Authority at the admission stage is confined to
   ascertaining the existence of debt and default.

   (iv) The documentary evidence upon which the
   Adjudicating Authority may record its satisfaction
   admits of a hierarchy. At the first tier stands a record
   of default issued by an Information Utility, which is
   by itself sufficient and which creates a presumption
   of high evidentiary value, displaceable only by clear,
   cogent, credible and compelling material and not by


C.A. No. 12195/2025                            Page 47 of 50
    bare denial or bookkeeping disagreement. At the
    second tier stands the other documentary material
    enumerated in Part V of Form 1 of the Insolvency and
    Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority)
    Rules, 2016 and its analogues which inter-alia
    includes loan agreements, statements of account,
    balance confirmations, acknowledgements of liability,
    and contemporaneous correspondence, which, taken
    collectively, may establish default upon the summary
    standard governing Section 7.

    (v) Profitability is neither legally relevant to, nor
    economically probative of, the capacity to service debt.
    The Code proceeds upon the principle of timely
    intervention rather than terminal insolvency, and
    adopts ‘default’ under Section 3(12) of the Code, not
    commercial or balance-sheet insolvency, as the
    jurisdictional trigger.

    (vi) Upon the record in these appeals, a default above
    the threshold prescribed under Section 4 of the Code
    is established.

72. For the reasons aforesaid, this Court finds no merit in
    either of these appeals and are, therefore dismissed.

DIPANKAR DATTA, J.


I.       INTRODUCTION

1.      On the tip of Switzerland, sharing its borders with France and

        Germany, lies the city of Basel. Through this city runs the river Rhine.

        As the river winds through the city, the Bank for International

        Settlements (BIS), a pivotal institution at the heart of the global

        financial system, stands prominently on its bank.

2.      In or about 2008, a certain bank — the term used loosely at this

        juncture — collapsed. What followed therefrom led to a series of one

        of the biggest financial meltdowns in history, ripples of which were felt

        across the world. This led to, among other things, the enactment in

        2010 of the Basel III Capital Regulations or the Basel III framework by

        the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision at the BIS. The Reserve

        Bank of India1 has implemented this framework through its Master

        Circular – Basel III Capital Regulations2.

3.      The present judgment interprets parts of the RBI’s mammoth Master

        Circular—possibly, the first of its kind by this Court to date. The novelty

        of this decision is less of a fascination and more of a formidable

        challenge, as we are mindful of the large-scale impact it may have,

        both immediate and gradual. Over the course of the last few decades,

        the banking and finance industry has ballooned into a sector worth

     billions. To a large extent, the RBI regulates this space. Its rules,

     regulations, and guidelines are routinely subjected to interpretation by

     law firms, senior advocates, retired judges and the like. Seldom do

     these disputes reach this Court. This leads to challenges in judicial

     clarity over matters of fiscal nature. Keeping all of this in mind, we now

     approach the matter at hand.

II. THE FACTS

4.   A judgment and order dated 20th January, 20233, passed by the High

     Court of Judicature at Bombay4 is impugned before us. The impugned

     Rs. 3,000 crore. On 18th October, 2017, a further tranche of AT-1 Bonds

     was issued for Rs. 5,415 crore. For both sets of AT-1 Bonds, Axis

     Trustee Services Limited7 was appointed as the trustee company. The

     AT-1 Bonds were regulated by the Master Circular.

6.   Since the financial position of YES BANK underwent a steep decline, on

     under section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 8 till 3rd April,

III. PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THIS COURT

10. Hearings on these appeals have spanned over several days, with

       several versions and iterations of written notes and submissions,

       compilations of documents and precedents being filed before and after

       and learned senior counsel Mr. Shyam Divan and Mr. Balbir Singh for

       YES BANK and its Administrator, respectively, who assailed the

       and other counsel appearing for the respondents, as well as the party-

IV. ANALYSIS

ISSUE A: WRITING DOWN AND ITS FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS

13. Appellants contend that if the impugned judgment is allowed to stand,

     it would trigger a severe financial avalanche; not just for YES BANK but

     for the entire banking system, undoing the very reconstruction

     exercise meant to lift YES BANK out of the financial crisis it faced.

14. Respondents, conversely, contend that YES BANK’s financial position has

     since risen well above regulatory levels, and that the impugned

     judgment — which struck down the Administrator’s decision to write

     down the AT-1 Bonds — should therefore be sustained. After SBI

     infused funds under the Reconstruction Scheme, YES BANK’s share price

     rose; and once the Scheme’s three-year lock-in period expired, SBI

     sold its majority stake in YES BANK at a substantial profit14. All parties,

     the respondents contend, have gained from the exercise.

15. The issue does not brook a short-cut; hence, we do not propose to end

     the lis by simply taking note of events subsequent to the impugned

     judgment and close the matter. We are reminded of a decision of this

     Court in Yash Deep Trexim Private Limited v. Namokar Vinimay

     the lis which unfolds before us calls for a resolution taking into

     consideration the position and circumstances that stood on the date

     when the Administrator ordered the AT-1 Bonds to be written down,

     i.e., on 14th March, 2020. Trite it is, in cases of challenge to an

     administrative action, the validity of such action must be tested as it

41. Before parting with this segment of the discussion, we place on record

    reliance placed by Mr. Divan and Mr. Singh upon sub-clause (1) of

    clause 6 of the Reconstruction Scheme which sought to preserve the

    efficacy of the bonds in the same manner before its commencement.

    They further contended that the Reconstruction Scheme did not

    abrogate the Administrator's inherent power to execute a write-down

    of the AT-1 Bonds. While it is true that the Administrator's residuary

    powers are preserved under the aforementioned clause, such a general

                                    17
    savings provision does not, by itself, confer the specific authority to

    write down the AT-1 Bonds after YES BANK came to be reconstructed. A

    definitive mechanism governing the treatment of AT-1 Bonds is

    prescribed by the Master Circular and the respective Information

    Memoranda, stipulating a separate and distinct procedural framework

    for each issuance in strict conformity with the Master Circular. It is a

    settled legal principle that a power not specifically conferred cannot be

    implicitly vested through a general, omnibus savings clause. To that

    extent, we rule against YES BANK and the Administrator.

42. Thus, the High Court correctly held that the Administrator could not

    have written down the Bonds in contravention of the Reconstruction

    Scheme.

ISSUE C: THE MASTER CIRCULAR, THE INFORMATION MEMORANDA AND THE

ADMINISTRATOR’S ACT OF WRITING DOWN THE AT-1 BONDS

43. It has been contended by all the appellants that notwithstanding the

    finally published Reconstruction Scheme, the Administrator was always

    empowered to write down the AT-1 Bonds. The specific contention of

    the appellants was that the Administrator acting under Section 36ACA

    of the BR Act and under the Information Memoranda of the AT-1 Bonds

    was empowered to write them down, in terms of the conditions

    stipulated therein. It was further contended that even if the

    Reconstruction Scheme did not provide for writing down the bonds,

    that in itself would not preclude the Administrator from exercising such

    power.



                                    18
44. We proceed to consider this issue unaffected by the outcome of the

       part discussed before, which is unfavourable to the appellants.

45. The contention raised must be examined from two perspectives: first,

       the conditions that empowered the Administrator to write down the

       bonds; and secondly, whether the conditions that were required to be

       satisfied in the exercise of such power. To do so, we first examine the

       Master Circular and the Information Memorandum to the extent

       relevant for the present purpose.

46. The Master Circular, under paragraph 4, divides regulatory capital of a

       bank in 2 parts: Tier 1 Capital and Tier 2 Capital. Tier 1 Capital is

       termed as the ‘going-concern capital’, whereas Tier 2 Capital is termed

       ‘gone-concern capital’. As is self-explanatory, going-concern capital

       can absorb losses without triggering a bank’s insolvency, whereas

       gone-concern capital absorbs losses in the event of the bank’s

       liquidation.

47. Tier 1 Capital is further divided into Common Equity Tier 122 and

       Additional Tier 123. Under the Master Circular, a bank must maintain

       total Tier 1 Capital equal to at least 7% of its Risk Weighted Assets

       (RWAs). Of this, at least 5.5% must be in the form of CET1. What

       constitutes CET 1 Capital is provided in clause 4.2.3 of the Master

       Circular read with Annex 1 thereof. The remaining 1.5% may,

       optionally, be met through AT1 Capital; which means that a bank is

23
     AT1

    not required to have any AT1 Capital at all and may choose to meet

    the entire 7% requirement through CET1 alone.

48. AT1 capital may be issued in various forms, such as Perpetual Non-

    Cumulative Preference Shares (PNCPS) or debt capital instruments, as

    in the present case. As long as an instrument complies with the

    conditions stipulated for it in the Master Circular, it can be reckoned

    towards AT1 capital. Here, Annex 4 of the Master Circular provides the

    criteria for issuance of the bonds.

49. Annex 16 of the Master Circular has been extensively relied upon by

    counsel for the parties; for that reason, we examine its components at

    this juncture.

50. Annex 16 provides the loss absorbency feature of the AT1 instruments.

    It further specifies two trigger events at which the loss absorbency

    feature may be exercised viz. (i) Pre-Specified Trigger Level; and (ii)

    Point of Non-Viability.

51. As per clause 2 of Annex 16, the Pre-Specified Trigger Level is reached

    when a bank's CET1 ratio falls below 6.125% of RWA (in case of YES

    BANK, 5.5% before 31st March, 2019, and 6.125% on or after that date,

    as per the Information Memorandum). This 6.125% threshold

    comprises the minimum CET1 requirement (5.5%) plus 25% of the

    capital conservation buffer of 2.5%, i.e., 0.625%.

52. Thus, the moment YES BANK’s CET1 ratio fell below the threshold of

    6.125%, YES BANK had the option to convert or write down the AT1

    instruments.

54. Thus, despite having the option but not the obligation to convert or

    write down the bonds, YES BANK chose not to. We do not intend to

61. The definition of ‘reconstructed bank’ was pressed upon us, repeatedly,

    by learned senior counsel for the appellants to contend that the

    reconstruction     process   of   YES   BANK    did   not   start   until   the

    Reconstruction Scheme was published in the Gazette, and that the

    right to write down the AT-1 Bonds arose only thereafter. Responding

    to our query as to when would the reconstruction exercise stand

    completed, the answer given was: not until every obligation under the

    Reconstruction Scheme had been discharged — meaning the exercise

    would continue until the last act under the Reconstruction Scheme was



                                       23
    performed, which might well be three years after the Scheme’s

    notification.

62. Relying on the definition of a ‘reconstructed bank’, Mr. Divan submitted

    that reconstruction of the reconstructed bank is a continuous process

    in terms of the Reconstruction Scheme. The contention advanced was

    that   the   reconstruction   process   did   not   commence   until   the

    Reconstruction Scheme was published in the Gazette, and more

    crucially, it remains ongoing until every obligation under the Scheme

    is completely discharged. On this premise, it was argued that the

    power to write down the AT-1 Bonds would continue to subsist with the

    Administrator until such time the reconstructed bank is fully

    reconstructed.

63. This part of the controversy turns on an incorrect interpretation of

    Clause 2.15 of Annex 16 of the Master Circular. The trigger viz. the

    point of non-viability is deemed to have been reached when the

    relevant authorities decide to reconstruct YES BANK, and in such an

    event the AT-1 Bonds ought to have been written down before the

    initial step of the reconstitution/reconstruction happened, i.e., the

    Reconstruction Scheme came into force. The preposition ‘before’ can

    only mean before the Reconstruction Scheme takes effect. True, the

    effects of a reconstruction scheme may run for years together; but

    that, by itself, cannot be read as empowering the relevant authority to

    write down the AT-1 Bonds at any point within the following three

    years. Had the intention been otherwise, the clause ought to have read

    “before reconstitution is complete”. We cannot by taking the aid of any

                                     24
    tool of interpretation read words in the relevant clause which are

    conspicuous by its absence. To read the clause in its present form in

    the manner urged by Mr. Divan would not only defeat the very object

    of the AT-1 Bonds but would produce an inherent absurdity, leaving

    investors to wonder at what point the guillotine blade might fall.

64. History bears this out. In the counter-affidavit filed by one of the

    respondents, i.e., 63 Moons Technologies Limited, a similar scenario

    involving a pari materia clause has been placed on record. Lakshmi

    Vilas Bank Limited was amalgamated with DBS Bank India Limited,

    and the information memorandum for its bonds — Basel III compliant

    Tier 2 Bonds — contained a similar clause, activating the trigger for

    writing down the bonds upon amalgamation / reconstitution. The

    amalgamation scheme was published in the Gazette on 25th November,

    2020, and was due to come into force on 27th November, 2020. The

    bonds worth Rs. 318.20 crore were written down by the administrator

    in that case on 26th November, 2020, a day ahead of the amalgamation

    scheme coming into force — in other words, before the amalgamation

    took effect. Why the same course was not adopted remains

    unexplained.

appropriate measures are taken to revive its operations and thus, enable it
to continue as a going concern. The difficulties faced by the Bank should be
such that these are likely to result in financial losses and raising the
Common Equity Tier 1 capital of the Bank should be considered as the most
appropriate way to prevent the Bank from turning non-viable. Such
measures would include write-off of non-equity regulatory capital in
combination with or without other measures as considered appropriate by
the Reserve Bank.


                                 28
       The Bank facing financial difficulties and approaching a PONV will be
       deemed to achieve viability if within a reasonable time in the opinion of RBI,
       it will be able to come out of the present difficulties if appropriate measures
       are taken to revive it. The measures including augmentation of equity
       capital through write off of Bonds/ public sector injection of funds are likely
       to:
       a. Restore depositors'/investors' confidence;
       b. Improve rating /creditworthiness of the Bank and thereby improve its
       borrowing capacity and liquidity and reduce cost of funds; and
       c. Augment the resource base to fund balance sheet growth in the case of
       fresh injection of funds.


       The trigger at PONV will be evaluated both at consolidated and solo level
       and breach at either level will trigger write-off.
                                                                        (emphasis ours)


69. On a reading of clauses 56 and 57, the pre-specified trigger, as

     mentioned above is reached when the CET1 ratio falls below the

     specified minimum. At that threshold, the Bank may choose whether

     to write off, write down, or convert the bonds, and which of the bonds

     are to be treated in which way, as per the options available in the

     Information Memorandum. However, once the point of non-viability is

     reached, or the Bank approaches non-viability, it no longer retains that

     discretion — it is then the RBI which determines, as per the standards

     set out in the Master Circular, whether the Bank is approaching or has

     reached the point of non-viability24, and it is then the RBI which must

     write down the Bonds.


24
   Annex 16, Clause 3. Minimum requirements to ensure loss absorbency of Non-equity
regulatory capital instruments at the point of non-viability
I. Mode of Loss Absorption and Trigger Event
3.1 The terms and conditions of all non-common equity Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital
instruments issued by the banks in India must have a provision that requires such
instruments, at the option of Reserve Bank of India, to either be written off or converted
into common equity upon the occurrence of the trigger event, called the Point of Non-
Viability (PONV)’ Trigger’ stipulated below:
…

                                           29
70. In the present case, admittedly, the point of non-viability was deemed

     to have been triggered when the relevant authorities decided to

     reconstruct YES BANK or even earlier. No sooner was the point of non-

     viability triggered than the RBI was required to write down the Bonds.

     Yet it was not the RBI that decided to write down the Bonds, but the

     Administrator appointed by the RBI, who wrote them down and

     communicated the same to the stock exchanges. The question is

     whether the Administrator can be said to have exercised the power

     vested in the RBI. We hold he cannot.

71. The Administrator exercises power under section 36ACA of the BR Act,

     the relevant portion of which reads as follows:

      36ACA. Supersession of Board of Directors in certain cases.—
      (1) Where the Reserve Bank is satisfied, in consultation with the Central
      Government, that in the public interest or for preventing the affairs of any
      banking company being conducted in a manner detrimental to the interest
      of the depositors or any banking company or for securing the proper
      management of any banking company, it is necessary so to do, the Reserve
      Bank may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, by order, supersede the
      Board of Directors of such banking company for a period not exceeding six
      months as may be specified in the order:
      Provided that the period of supersession of the Board of Directors may be
      extended from time to time, so, however, that the total period shall not
      exceed twelve months.
      (2) The Reserve Bank may, on supersession of the Board of Directors of the
      banking company under sub-section (1) appoint in consultation with the
      Central Government for such period as it may determine, an Administrator
      (not being an officer of the Central Government or a State Government)
      who has experience in law, finance, banking, economics or accountancy.
      (3) The Reserve Bank may issue such directions to the Administrator as it
      may deem appropriate and the Administrator shall be bound to follow such
      directions.
      (4) Upon making the order of supersession of the Board of Directors of a
      banking company, notwithstanding anything contained in the Companies
      Act, 1956 (1 of 1956),—


3.5 The amount of non-equity capital to be converted/ written-off will be determined by
RBI.

                                          30
     (a) the chairman, managing director and other directors shall, as from the
     date of supersession, vacate their offices as such;
     (b) all the powers, functions and duties which may, by or under the
     provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956) or this Act, or any other
     law for the time being in force, be exercised and discharged by or on behalf
     of the Board of Directors of such banking company, or by a resolution
     passed in general meeting of such banking company, shall, until the Board
     of Directors of such banking company is reconstituted, be exercised and
     discharged by the Administrator appointed by the Reserve Bank under sub-
     section (2):
     Provided that the power exercised by the Administrator shall be valid
     notwithstanding that such power is exercisable by a resolution passed in
     the general meeting of such banking company.
     (5) The Reserve Bank may constitute, in consultation with the Central
     Government, a committee of three or more persons who have experience
     in law, finance, banking, economics or accountancy to assist the
     Administrator in the discharge of his duties.
     …
                                                                (emphasis ours)


72. Thus, an administrator appointed under the BR Act has to act squarely

    within the four corners of the powers conferred upon him under the

    statute. He acts as a substitute for the Board of Directors, to run the

    company    in an    efficient   manner.   Any act performed by the

    administrator beyond the powers clothed upon him would be wholly

    illegal and void.

73. Thus, as per the Information Memorandum read with the Master

    Circular, there were 2 triggers for the bonds to be written down/written

    off. The first was for YES BANK to exercise; which it admittedly did not.

    The second was for the RBI to exercise which, not only did it express

    its intention not to—by eliminating the clause providing for writing

    down—but chose not to exercise it at all. The Administrator could not

    have assumed the regulatory role of the RBI and exercise a power

    which it did not have at all.

                                      31
74. Mr. Divan, in his signature tenor, attempted his best to emphasize on

    the necessity of ‘bail in’ and ‘bail out’ as an integral part of the

    reconstruction scheme. He contended that either of these events, by

    itself, could not bring back YES BANK to life again and restore the CET1

    ratio. A combined effort, first by writing down the bonds, and the

    subsequent infusion of funds by SBI—the chronology being of

    essence—was necessary to revive YES BANK. This submission was

    adopted by Mr. Mehta.

75. It may well be true that both of these events were necessary to revive

    YES BANK. However, mere necessity cannot possibly circumvent the

    manner in which the write down ought to have been exercised. This

    was required to be done in terms of the Master Circular only. The bail

    in and bail out events merely provided a right to write down the bonds,

    not the manner.

76. The pressing questions before us — to which the appellants ostensibly

    proffer no answer — are these: Was SBI not aware of the Draft

    Scheme, the Reconstruction Scheme, and the absence of the clause

    for writing down in the Reconstruction Scheme, when it was the one

    infusing funds for equity? Was the RBI, the regulator, not aware of the

    consequences of not retaining the write down clause in the

    Reconstruction Scheme? Was the RBI and the Administrator appointed

    by the RBI not aware as to who had the authority to write down the

    AT-1 Bonds as per the Master Circular? Was the Central Government

    not aware that the bonds had not yet been not written down when the

    Reconstruction Scheme was notified?

                                    32
77. These questions left unanswered answer the disjunct in the entire

    process carried out by the RBI, the Administrator and YES BANK. The

    question is not whether the AT-1 Bonds could have been or ought to

    have been written down off. The question is the manner in which it was

    done, de hors the Master Circular and the Information Memoranda. A

    conscious decision by the Central Government while approving the

    Reconstruction Scheme by deleting the clause from the Draft Scheme,

    evidently in favour of the bondholders, came to be dismantled at the

    hands of the Administrator.

78. The triumvirate of the RBI, the Administrator, and of course, YES BANK,

    in conducting the entire affair of dealing with the bonds worth more

    than 8,514 crore is, to put it mildly, questionable. Putting the investors

    to such uncalled-for risk, could have well been avoided. The purpose

    of the AT-1 Bonds is imperative: it acts as a safety barrier to the Bank

    from collapsing altogether. That purpose could have been served had

    the RBI and YES BANK acted in accordance with the terms of the Master

    Circular. The RBI was a mere bystander, allowing the CET1 ratio of YES

    BANK to drop to an astonishing low of 0.6% while the business of YES

    BANK was being carried out in a clandestine manner. It cannot be

    denied that material irregularities in functioning of YES BANK were

    noticed much prior; criminal prosecution has also been initiated

    against the personnel of YES BANK. However, to have the investors at

    the receiving end of the administrative lapses would be highly unfair.

79. We also note that the Master Circular specifies the classes of investors

    to whom AT1 instruments may be offered including, among others,

                                     33
      mutual funds and insurance companies. The AT-1 Bonds are high-risk

      securities and thus, as per the RBI, must be offered only to institutional

      investors. However, we find that YES BANK not only permitted but

      actively offered these instruments to individual investors in violation

      of the Master Circular. SEBI, in its counter affidavit, has stated that the

      bonds which were traded on BSE and NSE platforms were in

      compliance with the relevant SEBI regulations. In fact, SEBI also

      imposed penalty on a private wealth management firm as well as on

      the then Managing Director of YES BANK for facilitating sale of the bonds

      to private individual investors. However, the bonds which were offered

      directly by YES BANK to individual investors were beyond the purview

      of SEBI Regulations. An email dated 28th December, 2016, has been

      placed on record by the party in person before us, seemingly

      addressed by the Senior Manager – Financial Advisor of YES BANK,

      Chennai offering for sale the bonds to the individual investors. Many a

      bank has been hauled up by the regulator for offering such bonds to

      individual investors without necessary risk disclosures. A tighter

      scrutiny ought to have been exercised before luring individual investors

      to such high-risk securities.

IV.    CONCLUSION

80. Accordingly, for the foregoing reasons, we see no reason to interfere

      with the impugned judgment. The appeals are dismissed. Interim

      order, if any, stands vacated.




                                       34
81. The payment of annual coupon rate shall remain unaffected by the

    outcome of these appeals and must be made in terms of the

    Information Memoranda.

82. Parties are left to bear their own costs.

83. It is clarified that observations made are only for the purpose of

    decision on these appeals. Any pending proceeding may be taken to

    its logical conclusion uninfluenced by any such observation.

19. We have considered the rival submissions and have perused

20. The issues which arise for consideration are as follows:-

     (a)   whether the Borrower is entitled to refund of the entire
