21. Now, we proceed to deal with the issues ad seriatim.

     ANALYSIS

     (a) WHETHER THE BORROWER IS ENTITLED TO REFUND
     OF THE ENTIRE AMOUNT INCLUDING THE AMOUNT
     DEPOSITED BY THE BANK, IF SO, AT WHAT RATE OF
     INTEREST?

22. The entitlement of the Borrower to refund of the entire

     amount is required to be examined on the touchstone of the

     principle that no one shall be enriched at the expense of

     another. The principle is of ancient origin and finds

     expression in the maxim nemo debet locupletari ex aliena

     jactura, that is, no one ought to be enriched by the loss of

     another.

23. In India, the principle has a statutory home. Chapter V of the

     Indian Contract Act, 1872 (the Contract Act), comprising

     Sections 68 to 72, deals with “certain relations resembling

     those created by contract”. Section 70 of the Contract Act

     obliges a person who enjoys the benefit of a lawful, non-

     gratuitous act of another to compensate him. Section 72

                                                                14
       mandates that a person to whom money has been paid, or

       anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion, must repay

       or return it. Sections 64 and 65 require a benefit received

       under a contract which is rescinded, or which becomes void,

       to be restored to the person from whom it was received.

24. The elements of the Doctrine of Unjust Enrichment were

       identified by this Court in Mahabir Kishore v. State of

       Madhya Pradesh3, and it was held that the doctrine

       proceeds on the basis that it would be unjust to allow one

       person to retain a benefit received at the expense of another.

       Stated simply, ‘unjust enrichment’ means retention of a

       benefit by a person that is unjust or inequitable4. It has also

       been described as “the unjust retention of a benefit to the loss

       of another”5. A Bench of nine Judges of this Court applied the

       doctrine to claims for refund of duties and held that a

       claimant who has passed on the burden of a duty to others

       cannot recover it for himself, for he has suffered no loss6.

25. Three things follow. First, the doctrine is part of our law, both

       by statute and as a principle of equity. Second, it looks at the


3
  (1989) 4 SCC 1
4
  Sahakari Khand Udyog Mandal Ltd. v. Commissioner of Central Excise, (2005) 3 SCC 738
5
  Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India, (2011) 8 SCC 161
6
  Mafatlal Industries Ltd. v. Union of India, (1997) 5 SCC 536

                                                                                         15
      person who holds a benefit and asks whether, in conscience,

      he may keep it. Third, it is a doctrine of correction and not of

      reward. Restitution restores. It does not redistribute. It

      returns value to the person at whose expense it was received.

      It does not confer value on a person merely because he has

      been wronged.

26.   The law of contract compensates, it does not enrich. Even

      while enhancing the rate of interest payable to a buyer, this

      Court in Rajnesh Sharma (supra) cautioned that the

      objective of granting compensation cannot be altered such

      that it amounts to a windfall gain to the other party.

27. In the backdrop of the aforesaid well-settled legal principles,

      we advert to the facts of the case in hand. The transaction is

      triangular. The Builder received Rs.2,19,92,107/- (Rupees

      Two Crore Nineteen Lakh Ninety Two Thousand One Hundred

      Seven only) and gave nothing in return. The retention of that

      amount by the Builder is plainly unjust, and the Builder has

      rightly not disputed its liability to refund it. The real question

      is to whom the refund must go. The money came from two

      sources.   Admittedly,    the   Borrower     paid   a   sum     of

      Rs.51,11,576/- (Rupees Fifty One Lakh Eleven Thousand


                                                                     16
     Five Hundred Seventy Six only) to the Builder from his own

     funds. He also paid a sum of Rs.76,23,150/- (Rupees Seventy

     Six Lakh Twenty Three Thousand One Hundred Fifty only) to

     the Bank, comprising Rs.26,23,150/- (Rupees Twenty Six

     Lakh Twenty Three Thousand One Hundred Fifty only) paid

     towards interest up to March, 2013, Rs.20,00,000/- (Rupees

     Twenty Lakh only) paid on 23.06.2021 and Rs.30,00,000/-

     (Rupees Thirty Lakh only) paid on 14.07.2021. Thus, the

     Borrower paid a total sum of Rs.1,27,34,726/- (Rupees One

     Crore Twenty Seven Lakh Thirty Four Thousand Seven

     Hundred Twenty Six only) out of his own pocket. The

     remaining amount was paid by the Bank to the Builder out

     of the loan, and has not been repaid by the Borrower.

28. It is true that under Recital (H) and Clause 4 of the Tripartite

     Agreement, a disbursal to the Builder is deemed to be a

     disbursal to the Borrower. That fiction, however, serves a

     limited purpose. It fastens the obligation to repay the loan on

     the Borrower, though the money never passed through his

     hands. It does not convert borrowed money, which remains

     unpaid, into the Borrower’s own money. The Commission

     nevertheless directed refund of Rs.2,19,92,107/- (Rupees


                                                                  17
    Two Crore Nineteen Lakh Ninety Two Thousand One Hundred

    Seven only) to the Borrower along with interest, without any

    reference to the lender whose money it largely was. Payment

    of the entire amount to the Borrower, while the loan remains

    outstanding and the claim of the Bank is in dispute, would

    place in his hands a sum which he has not paid. It amounts

    to unjust enrichment, which is impermissible in law. We,

    therefore, hold that the Borrower is entitled, in his own right,

    to refund of a sum of Rs.1,27,34,726/- (Rupees One Crore

    Twenty Seven Lakh Thirty Four Thousand Seven Hundred

    Twenty Six only).

29. Now we examine the claim of the Borrower for interest. The

    relevant extract of Clause 24 of the Agreement for Sale dated

    21.10.2009 reads as under: -

            “24. The Builder/Promoter shall give
            possession of the said Residential
            Apartment to the purchaser on or before
            30th    day    of    June,    2011.    The
            Builder/Promoter shall be entitled to a
            grace period of 6 months if he fails or
            neglects to give possession of the said
            Residential Apartment to the Purchaser on
            or before the date aforesaid on account of
            reasons beyond its control. In the event,
            the Builder/Promoter fails to handover the
            possession of the Residential Apartment to
            the Purchaser beyond the said grace period


                                                                  18
            of 6 months, then and in that event, the
            Builder/Promoter shall, on demand, be
            liable to refund to the Purchaser the
            compensation calculated at the rate of 12
            percent per annum on the amounts paid
            by the Purchaser from the date of expiry of
            such grace period of 6 months …
            Alternatively, on such expiry of the said
            grace period of 6 months, the Purchaser
            may by giving notice in writing to the
            builder elect to terminate this Agreement
            and in such event, the Builder/Promoter
            shall on demand be liable to refund to the
            Purchaser the amounts already received
            by the Builder/Promoter in respect of the
            said premises with simple interest at 12
            percent per annum from the date the
            Builder/Promoter received such demand
            till the date of refund. …”

30. Thus, by Clause 24 of the Agreement for Sale, the parties

    themselves have fixed the rate of interest at 12% per annum.

    Clause 24 of the Agreement for Sale provides that the Builder

    must pay compensation at the rate of 12% per annum in case

    it fails to deliver the apartment in time, and that in case the

    purchaser terminates the agreement, the Builder must

    refund the amount to the purchaser with simple interest at

    the rate of 12% per annum. The Borrower himself, in his

    complaint, claimed interest at the rate of 12% per annum up

    to the date of the complaint. The claim of the Borrower for

    interest at the rate of 18% per annum, founded on Clause 19


                                                                 19
       of the Agreement for Sale and on the decision in Rajnesh

       Sharma (supra), is of no assistance to him. Clause 19 does

       not stand alone; Clause 24 stands beside it and specifically

       governs the consequence of the Builder’s default. In Rajnesh

       Sharma (supra), this Court enhanced the rate of interest

       from 9% to 18% in view of the conduct of the builder, who

       had kept the buyer waiting for over a decade and had charged

       him interest at 18% for delayed payments. This Court,

       however, made it clear that what is reasonable varies from

       case to case, and that the rate of interest charged by the

       builder cannot be granted to the buyer as a rule of thumb.

       This Court has also held that interest at 18% cannot be

       awarded as a uniform rule, and that the relief must depend

       on the facts of each case7. Where the parties have agreed

       upon a particular consequence of delay in handing over

       possession, require strong reasons to depart from it8.

31. For the aforementioned reasons, and especially in view of

       Clause 24 of the Agreement for Sale, the Borrower is entitled




7
 Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Balbir Singh, (2004) 5 SCC 65
8
 DLF Homes Panchkula Pvt. Ltd. v. D.S. Dhanda, (2020) 16 SCC 318 and Greater Mohali Area
Development Authority v. Anupam Garg, 2025 SCC OnLine SC 1312

                                                                                     20
    to simple interest at the rate of 12% per annum. The interest

    shall run from the date of each payment.

32. Accordingly, issue (a) is answered by stating that the

    Borrower is entitled to refund of a sum of Rs. 1,27,34,726/-

    (Rupees One Crore Twenty Seven Lakh Thirty Four Thousand

    Seven Hundred Twenty Six only), that is the amount

    deposited by him along with interest at the rate of 12% per

    annum from the date of each deposit till the amount is paid

    to the Borrower.

    (b) WHETHER THE BORROWER IS ENTITLED TO
    COMPENSATION, INCLUDING REIMBURSEMENT OF THE
    RENT CLAIMED BY HIM?

33. The complaint made by the Borrower was not confined to

    refund of the amount and interest. The Borrower had sought

    reimbursement of rent of Rs.7,97,895/- (Rupees Seven Lakh

    Ninety Seven Thousand Eight Hundred Ninety Five only) for

    the period from 01.07.2011 to 30.04.2013 and further rent

    thereafter, and had also claimed a sum of Rs.15,00,000/-

    (Rupees Fifteen Lakh only) for mental agony and harassment.

    The Commission reproduced these prayers in its order and

    even observed that the Borrower was entitled to refund of the

    amount deposited along with compensation. Yet, the


                                                               21
          operative part of its order grants no compensation against the

          Builder. The prayers were not adverted to at all. The grievance

          of the Borrower in this regard is, to that extent, well founded.

34. The power to award compensation flows from Section 14(1)(d)

          read with Section 22 of the Act. In Lucknow Development

          Authority v. M.K. Gupta9, this Court explained that the Act

          enables the consumer to claim, and the forum to award, not

          only the value of the goods or services but also compensation

          for the injustice suffered. In Ghaziabad Development

          Authority (supra), this Court held that what is awarded

          under the Act is compensation, that is, a recompense for the

          loss or injury, and that it “necessarily has to be based on a

          finding of loss or injury and has to correlate with the amount

          of loss or injury”. The Court illustrated that where possession

          is not given, the loss may be determined on the basis of the

          rent which could have been earned, or the rent actually paid

          by the consumer. In Bangalore Development Authority v.

          Syndicate Bank10, this Court held that where possession is

          not delivered within the stipulated time, the allottee is

          entitled to refund of the amount paid with reasonable interest

9
    (1994) 1 SCC 243
10
     (2007) 6 SCC 711

                                                                        22
           from the date of payment, and may in addition be entitled to

           compensation, as may be decided with reference to the facts

           of each case. The power, however, is to award compensation

           for loss or injury suffered by the consumer due to the

           negligence of the opposite party. It is a power to compensate

           for a loss which is proved and which flows from the default.

           It is not a power to award every expense which the consumer

           has incurred during the pendency of the dispute. Damages

           for contractual breach are generally compensatory; an award

           which surpasses actual loss enters the domain of a gain-

           based remedy, and the court must take a balanced approach

           so as to ensure right compensation.11

35. Before this Court, the claim for rent has grown far beyond

           what was initially claimed before the Commission. In the

           rejoinder affidavit, for the first time, the rent at Rs.38,000/-

           (Rupees Thirty Eight Thousand only) per month from July,

           2011 to July, 2013, and the rent at Rs.65,000/- (Rupees

           Sixty Five Thousand only) per month from August, 2013 to

           October, 2022 has been claimed. The aforesaid sum cannot

           be permitted to be claimed for the first time in these Civil


11
     Fortune Infrastructure v. Trevor D’lima, (2018) 5 SCC 442

                                                                         23
          Appeals. For the reasons which follow, we are not persuaded

          to compensate the Borrower for the rent so claimed.

36. Firstly, the Act has no provision corresponding to provisions

          in other branches of law, such as Rent Control legislations

          which statutorily recognises the right of a tenant to claim

          rent, in case he hands over the possession of the tenanted

          premises for reconstruction/rebuilding.

37. Secondly, the award of rent in addition to interest on the full

          refund would amount to double compensation for the same

          default. Interest at 12% per annum is awarded precisely

          because the Borrower was deprived of the use of his money.

          Had that money been with him, he could have applied it to

          secure a home of his own. In D.S. Dhanda (supra), this

          Court, relying on Irrigation Department, Government of

          Orissa v. G.C. Roy,12, held that a person deprived of the use

          of money to which he is legitimately entitled has a right to be

          compensated for that deprivation, which may be called

          interest, compensation or damages; that “such interest will

          take into its ambit, the consequences of delay in not handing

          over his possession”; and that an award “under various heads


12
     (1992) 1 SCC 508

                                                                       24
     in respect of the same default is not sustainable”. The Court

     further held that the consumer fora “cannot award interest

     and/or compensation by applying rule of thumb”. To award

     him both, the return on the money which would have bought

     him a home and the rent which he paid for want of one would

     be to compensate him twice for the same loss.

38. Thirdly, the claim travels beyond the pleadings and the proof.

     The complaint quantified the rent at Rs.7,97,895/- (Rupees

     Seven Lakh Ninety Seven Thousand Eight Hundred Ninety

     Five only) for the period up to 30.04.2013. The figures for the

     subsequent period, running into several lakhs every year, are

     stated for the first time in a rejoinder affidavit in this Court,

     supported only by a bank statement for the year 2021. No

     lease deed, rent receipt or other evidence of the tenancy was

     placed before the Commission. A claim of this magnitude

     cannot be adjudicated in a statutory appeal on the strength

     of averments made in a rejoinder.

39. Fourthly, and more fundamentally, the Borrower elected his

     remedy. Clause 24 of the Agreement for Sale provides two

     alternative remedies upon the Builder’s failure to deliver

     possession. The purchaser may stay in the project and


                                                                    25
    receive compensation at the rate of 12% per annum till

    possession is handed over; or he may terminate the

    agreement and receive a refund of the amount paid with

    simple interest at the rate of 12% per annum. By filing the

    complaint on 13.05.2013 and seeking a refund, the Borrower

    chose the second course. Having chosen to give up the

    apartment, he cannot claim, in addition, the rent which he

    would have saved had he taken possession of it. From the

    date of that election, the cost of housing himself is not a loss

    caused by the non-delivery of an apartment which he no

    longer wished to have. It is a cost which every person must

    bear, whether he owns a home or rents one. The obligation of

    the Builder thereafter was to return his money with interest,

    and that obligation is being enforced.

40. Lastly, the claim is inconsistent with the Borrower’s own

    case. By his letter dated 03.11.2012, the Borrower quantified

    his loss as the rent which he could have earned by letting out

    the apartment, at about Rs.1,50,000/- (Rupees One Lakh

    Fifty Thousand only) per month. The same apartment, for the

    same period, cannot be the source both of rent which the

    Borrower would have received and of rent which he was


                                                                  26
    compelled to pay. Further, the Borrower has stated that he

    resided in rented premises until he purchased another

    apartment.    Under    Section   73   of   the   Contract   Act,

    compensation is payable for loss which naturally arose in the

    usual course of things from the breach, and, by the

    Explanation to that Section, the means which existed of

    remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance

    must be taken into account. A purchaser who has elected to

    take his money back, and who has the benefit of interest on

    it, cannot claim rent indefinitely thereafter.

41. The claim of compensation quantified by the Borrower

    himself in the consumer complaint filed on 13.05.2013 was

    Rs. 7,97,895/- (Rupees Seven Lakh Ninety Seven Thousand

    Eight Hundred Ninety Five only). The Borrower has been

    subjected to prolonged uncertainty, having paid about 95%

    of the consideration by July 2011 and having been kept out

    of both the apartment and his money for over fifteen years.

    The Borrower has been deprived of the benefit of escalation

    in the price of the apartment and therefore, compensation, in

    such a case has to be higher than the return of the money

    deposited by the Borrower. The quantum of compensation


                                                                  27
           depends on the facts of each case. Having regard to the

           totality of circumstances and in order to avoid prolonged

           inquiry, at this distance of time, we deem it appropriate to

           award a sum of Rs. 15,00,000/- (Rupees Fifteen Lakh only)

           to the Borrower as compensation. The said amount shall be

           towards full and final satisfaction of all the claims of the

           Borrower against the Builder towards rent, mental agony,

           harassment and litigation expenses. Issue (b) is answered

           accordingly.

(c) WHETHER THE BANK WAS DEFICIENT IN RENDERING
SERVICE TO THE BORROWER?


42. Section 2(1)(g) of the Act defines “deficiency” as any fault,

           imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality,

           nature and manner of performance which is required to be

           maintained under any law, or which has been undertaken to

           be performed in pursuance of a contract or otherwise, in

           relation to any service. Deficiency is a matter of proof. The

           burden of proving it lies on the person who alleges it13. This

           Court has reiterated that the initial burden of proving

           deficiency in service is on the complainant, and that the


13
     Ravneet Singh Bagga v. KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, (2000) 1 SCC 66

                                                                        28
           burden shifts to the opposite party only when that initial

           burden is discharged.14

43. The Borrower discharged his initial burden. He repeatedly

           asked the Bank to verify the progress of construction. By e-

           mail      dated       21.03.2010,            he     sought    the   Bank’s   own

           assessment of the construction activity. On 24.05.2011, he

           told the Builder that the progress made did not justify further

           payment; yet the last tranche was released in July, 2011. By

           a letter dated 22.06.2012 and e-mails dated 29.10.2012 and

           30.10.2012, he sought its inspection reports and an

           inspection by a third party. By 30.06.2011, when possession

           was due, the Builder had received about 95% of the

           consideration. Yet on 30.10.2012 the Bank itself reported the

           building to be only 90% ready, and the fire no-objection

           certificate came to be issued only in May, 2013. The burden

           then shifted to the Bank. Whether it verified the progress of

           construction before each disbursal was a fact especially

           within its knowledge. Although the Bank claimed, by its reply

           dated 02.05.2012, that its engineers had inspected the site

           before each release, it produced no inspection report before


14
     SGS (India) Ltd. v. Dolphin International Ltd., (2022) 19 SCC 442

                                                                                         29
     the Commission. Its written version was not taken on record,

     and it led no evidence. Its witness in the suit stated that such

     reports were not required. The fact that the thirteen tranches

     matched the stage-wise instalments in Clause 6 of the

     Agreement for Sale, or that the Borrower forwarded the

     Builder’s demands, indicates only that the Bank paid what

     was demanded. It does not show that the Bank verified the

     stage of construction, as its own letter of sanction obliged it

     to do.

44. The finding of deficiency recorded by the Commission is thus

     a finding of fact founded on the material on record. It is

     neither perverse nor based on no evidence. The compensation

     of Rs.2,00,000/- (Rupees Two Lakh only) awarded against the

     Bank is modest and commensurate with the deficiency. We

     find no ground to interfere with it, either at the instance of

     the Bank or at the instance of the Borrower. The finding of

     deficiency and the direction to the Bank to pay Rs.2,00,000/-

     (Rupees Two Lakh only) to the Borrower are accordingly

     upheld. Accordingly, issue (c) is answered.

     (d) THE RELIEF TO WHICH THE BANK IS ENTITLED TO
     IN THESE PROCEEDINGS



                                                                   30
45. These proceedings arise out of consumer complaint in which

     the claim of the Bank based on tripartite agreement cannot

     be examined. The Bank is entitled to recover the sum lawfully

     due to it from the Borrower. It is noteworthy that the Bank

     has already initiated proceedings for recovery of the amount

     due to it by filing a suit before the Commercial Court, which

     was dismissed, and its claim is now pending in appeal before

     the High Court. We, therefore, cannot examine the claim of

     the Bank in these proceedings; it is required to be adjudicated

     in the appeal pending before the High Court. The High Court

     shall decide the appeal on its own merits. All contentions of

     the Bank and the Borrower, including the contention of the

     Borrower regarding his liability under the loan, are left open.

46. Now, we deal with I.A. No. 95385 of 2026, by which Borrower

     seeks amendment of the cause title and the memo of parties.

     The Borrower not only seeks change of his name but also

     seeks to bring on record the present names of the

     respondents. The description of the respondents as proposed

     by the Borrower has been opposed by the respondents. We

     are, therefore, not inclined to permit to change the

     description of respondents. However, from the document


                                                                  31
    annexed with the application, we are satisfied that the name

    of the appellant has been changed from K. Madhusudhan

    Rao to Madhu Kudapa. The application is, therefore, allowed

    to the limited extent of permitting the Borrower to change his

    name in the cause title and the memo of parties. Accordingly,

    I.A. No. 95385 of 2026 is disposed of.

    CONCLUSION AND DIRECTIONS

47. For the foregoing reasons, the following directions are

    issued:-

    (i)    The Commission shall release to the Borrower, a sum of

           Rs.1,27,34,726/- (Rupees One Crore Twenty Seven

           Lakh Thirty Four Thousand Seven Hundred Twenty Six

           only) along with interest at the rate of 12% per annum

           from the date of respective deposits made by the

           Borrower to the Builder and the Bank till the date of

           payment.

    (ii)   The Commission shall release a further sum of

           Rs.15,00,000/- (Rupees Fifteen Lakh only) to the

           Borrower as compensation out of the said deposit,

           within a period of one month from today.




                                                                32
     (iii)   The remaining amount shall be kept by the Commission

             in an interest bearing account which shall abide by the

             decision of the appeal filed by the Bank.

     (iv)    The High Court shall decide the appeal pending before

             it without being influenced by any of the observations

             made herein, on its own merits.

48. The order of the Commission is modified accordingly. The

     Appeals are disposed of accordingly. There shall be no order

     as to costs.

49. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

ANALYSIS

15.   We have heard the learned senior counsels and have perused the

written submissions advanced on behalf of the State and the materials placed

on record. We have also carefully considered the challenge founded upon the

jurisdiction of the High Court to examine the validity of the said G.O. in

proceedings in which the original prayer was confined to the issuance of a

community certificate.


16.   The challenge before us, however, cannot be determined merely by

asking whether the High Court travelled beyond the prayer made in the writ

petition preferred by respondent no. 1. The validity and legal effect of the G.O.

have necessarily arisen for consideration because the very right claimed by

respondent no. 1 is founded upon it. A perusal of the record of proceedings

would project that the High Court, after noticing the G.O., impleaded the State

as a party, afforded it an opportunity to place its case, heard the learned

Additional Advocate General of the State and proceeded to adjudicate upon

the legal foundation of the relief claimed. The record itself shows that the High

Court, on 11.06.2026, took the view that the G.O. might not withstand

judicial scrutiny and thereupon impleaded the State.


17.   It is true that ordinarily a court should not pronounce upon the validity

of an instrument when the parties have not had notice of the challenge and




SLP (C) No.25507/2026                                               Page 7 of 40
no opportunity to meet it.8 The principle which underlines herein is one of

fairness wherein parties must know the case they are required to meet and a

court should not ordinarily grant relief on a ground which has neither been

pleaded nor put in issue. But the principle is not a mechanical prohibition

upon a Constitutional Court examining an instrument whose validity

becomes inseparable from the relief before it. The only question which is

crucial herein is whether the affected party had notice of the issue and a

meaningful opportunity to address it. As far as the present case is concerned,

the State was specifically impleaded after the High Court formed a prima facie

view concerning the validity of the G.O. A counter affidavit was filed and the

learned Additional Advocate General of the State appeared and addressed the

Court on the very question. The High Court expressly recorded that the

proceedings had, by then, reached the stage of final adjudication for the

purpose of testing the validity of the G.O.


18.    The present case is therefore distinguishable from a case where a Court,

without notice, converts an ordinary dispute into a constitutional challenge

and determines an issue on which the parties have neither pleaded nor led

submissions. The objection of the State based upon the absence of a formal

prayer consequently cannot, in the facts of the present case, prevent

examination of the G.O. Indeed, once the State itself defended the validity and

operation of the G.O. and relied upon it as the legal basis for respondent no.

1's entitlement, the Court could not be expected to grant relief on the

beyond examination.


19.      This now brings us to the substance of controversy in the present case.

However, before examining the validity and legal effect of the impugned G.O.,

it would be apposite to notice the religious and social framework within which

the controversy has arisen. This is necessary not to enter into matters of

theology as an end in themselves, but to appreciate the distinction between

religious identity, community affiliation and social status which lies at the

heart of the controversy. The question before us concerns the consequences

attributed by the impugned G.O. to a person's conversion to Islam and, in

particular, the manner in which such conversion is sought to be connected

with membership of a notified Backward Class Muslim community. The

answer to that question cannot be divorced from an understanding of the

concepts which the impugned G.O. seeks to bring together. We, therefore,

consider, at the outset, the relevant religious and social features before

turning to the constitutional and legal validity of the course adopted by the

State.


A.       THEOLOGY OF ISLAM

20.      Islam rests, in its foundational theological conception, upon the

equality of human beings and does not make birth, lineage or descent the

measure of human worth. The Holy Quran articulates this principle in clear

terms in Surah Al-Hujurat, Ayah (49:13)9:

                “O humanity! Indeed, We created you from a male and
                a female, and made you into peoples and tribes so that
                you may get to know one another. Surely the most

                                                    (emphasis supplied)

21.   The verse recognises the existence of peoples and tribes, but does not

attribute to such distinctions any inherent superiority or inferiority. The

criterion of nobility is expressly stated to be righteousness. The distinction,

therefore, is between an identity arising from one's birth or lineage and the

moral worth attributed to an individual; the former does not, in the conception

embodied in the verse, determine the latter.


22.   The same principle finds expression in the Farewell Sermon (Khubat al-

Hajjat) of the Holy Prophet Muhammad (Peace be upon him), wherein he is

recorded to have stated:

                “All mankind is from Adam and Eve. An Arab has no
                superiority over a non-Arab, nor does a non-Arab have
                any superiority over an Arab; a white person has no
                superiority over a black person, nor does a black
                person have any superiority over a white person,
                except by piety and good deeds. Learn that every
                Muslim is a brother to every Muslim and that the
                Muslims constitute one brotherhood.”10

23.   The foundational proposition is thus one of equality notwithstanding

differences of race, tribe, lineage or descent. The distinction which Islam

24.    The social organisation of Muslims in India, however, has historically

Ashraf were described as the “noble born”, while the Ajlaf and Arzal comprised

groups placed lower in the social hierarchy. These broad categories, however,

comprised a plurality of distinct groups and were not themselves

homogeneous communities.

and zat to describe a member of these groups. The evidence discussed by

noted sociologist Imtiaz Ahmad12 in his book titled ‘Caste and Social

several    instances,    associated      with   particular     occupations,      observed

endogamous practices and were constituted on the basis of birth. Membership

in such a group was consequently not ordinarily a matter of individual choice

or religious profession.

26.   The distinction between community and caste assumes particular

Arzal. These terms describe broad gradations of social position and

encompass numerous distinct communities. Within the Ashraf, for instance,

there were different groups associated with identities such as Sayyid, Shaikh,

Pathan and Qureshi, while the Ajlaf and Arzal categories likewise comprised

different communities with their own occupational, social and local identities.

The broad classification therefore cannot itself be treated as a description of

27.   At the same time, the fact that these communities were distinct does

not mean that their social organisation was devoid of hierarchical or

hereditary features. Among sections of Indian Muslims, membership in

particular   communities     could   be   substantially   hereditary;   particular

communities could be historically associated with particular occupations;

marriage could predominantly take place within the group; and groups could

occupy unequal positions in the local social order. These are features of social

stratification which cannot be disregarded merely because the foundational

religious doctrine is egalitarian.


28.   Nor does the existence of a hereditary occupational association,

considered by itself, establish the existence of caste. An occupation followed

by successive generations may, over time, become associated with the identity

of a community and may continue to influence matrimonial and social

relations even after individuals cease to practise that occupation. Hereditary

be treated as a sufficient test of caste in isolation.


29.    The comparison with the classical caste order must also take account

of the absence of a single, uniformly applicable religiously prescribed scheme

in the social organisation of Indian Muslims. The boundaries and status of

Muslim communities have not been uniformly fixed or equally rigid across

regions and groups. Social identities could, in particular circumstances, be

asserted, modified or reconfigured, including through processes of social

mobility and changes in claims to status and lineage.


30.    The possibility of such movement in social status has also been

examined in the sociological literature through the concept of ‘Ashrafisation’.

The expression ‘Ashrafisation’ as stated by sociologist Imtiaz Ahmad13 denotes

a process whereby individuals, families or groups occupying a relatively lower

position in the social hierarchy sought to enhance or reconstitute their social

standing through the adoption of the customs, manners, titles or genealogical

claims associated with the Ashraf (noble class). The concept illustrates that,

notwithstanding the existence of hierarchical distinctions, claims to social

status and lineage were not invariably immutable. Social position could, in

particular circumstances, be negotiated, asserted or reconstructed. This

possibility of upward social movement did not dissolve the underlying

hierarchy; rather, it demonstrates that hierarchy and mobility could coexist

31.   The position that emerges is consequently a nuanced one. Among

sections of Indian Muslims, there have existed communities whose

organisation displays several characteristics ordinarily associated with caste,

including hereditary membership, occupational association, endogamy and

graded social status. Such characteristics establish the existence of social

stratification and, in particular contexts, caste-like structures. They do not,

however, warrant treating Ashraf, Ajlaf and Arzal as three homogeneous

castes constituting a single and uniform system throughout Muslim society

in India.


32.   The distinction between religious prescription and social practice must

therefore be maintained. The Islamic conception reflected in the Quranic verse

and the Farewell Sermon of the Prophet, as discussed by us earlier, places

the criterion of human worth in righteousness and conduct, and not in race,

tribe or lineage. The social practices that developed among particular Muslim

communities in India may depart from, or stand in tension with, that

foundational conception. Their existence cannot, however, retrospectively

convert a social practice into a theological command; equally, the absence of

such a theological prescription cannot be taken to mean that caste-like forms

of social stratification did not develop among Indian Muslims.


33.   It is thus possible to recognise both propositions without contradiction.

That the egalitarian principle is foundational to Islam, and that Muslim

society in India has not been immune from social stratification. The

been wholly untouched by caste, nor that it has reproduced in every respect

the classical caste system. Rather, distinct Muslim communities have, in

varying degrees and in different regions, developed forms of hereditary social

stratification which may be analogous to caste, while remaining distinct

communities whose boundaries and social positions have not been uniformly

fixed.


34.      The foregoing discussion assumes significance when the effect of

conversion upon an existing claim to affirmative action is considered. The

persons professing Islam, nor whether a person who has converted from

suffered in the past. The anterior question is whether the social

circumstances which rendered a person backward in the social order from

which he has converted can continue, after conversion, to furnish the basis

of a constitutional claim to affirmative action. This, in turn, requires

consideration of the manner in which backwardness is understood for the

purposes of Article 16(4) of the Constitution and its relationship with the

social structure in which it arises.

36.   The aforesaid exposition also explains the significance of the

proposition in Indra Sawhney (supra) that caste cannot, by itself, be the sole

criterion for identifying a backward class. The proposition does not proceed

on the assumption that caste is merely one factor amongst several unrelated

considerations. In the Hindu social order, caste has historically constituted

the principal basis upon which social status and the attendant disabilities

have been organised and perpetuated. The requirement that other relevant

circumstances must also be taken into account serves a different purpose.

Mere membership of a caste cannot be treated as conclusive proof that every

individual belonging to it continues to suffer the social backwardness which

Article 16(4) of the Constitution seeks to address. A person belonging to a

caste historically regarded as backward may, by reason of education,

occupation, economic/social advancement or an elevation in social standing,

have ceased to suffer the disabilities which constitute the basis of affirmative

action. It is for this reason that the identification of a backward class cannot

rest upon caste alone, and that the other circumstances bearing upon the

continuance of social backwardness must also be examined. The exclusion of

the creamy layer is itself an illustration of this principle. The enquiry is thus

directed towards identifying those who continue to suffer the relevant social

disability and not towards treating caste membership as an immutable or

conclusive constitutional status for affirmative action.


37.   There is, however, a distinct question which did not arise for

consideration in Indra Sawhney (supra). That decision considered the

manner in which backward classes may be identified, including among non-

Hindus, and recognised that occupational groups, sects and denominations

among non-Hindus may, for historical reasons, constitute backward classes

under Article 16(4). It did not consider the effect of a change of religion upon

an existing claim to affirmative action founded upon the social backwardness

within the Hindu social order. The question before us is therefore not whether

persons professing a religion other than Hinduism can constitute a backward

class. They plainly may, where the constitutional requirements are

independently satisfied. The question is whether social backwardness arising

within one social order or religion can continue to furnish the same

constitutional entitlement upon a person's entry into another social order or

religion.


38.   The answer must necessarily have regard to the source of the social

backwardness in question. In the Hindu social order, caste has been the

foundational institution through which social hierarchy, birth-based status,

hereditary occupation, social intercourse and access to social and educational

opportunities have historically been structured. The several manifestations of

social backwardness may therefore present themselves in different forms such

as occupational, educational, economic or otherwise. But, apart from the

euphemism by which such manifestations may be described, their historical

and social foundation, where the backwardness in question is caste-based,

lies in the caste order itself. The fact that Indra Sawhney (supra) requires

considerations other than caste to be taken into account does not permit this

foundational fact to be disregarded.




SLP (C) No.25507/2026                                              Page 18 of 40
39.      It is in this context that the effect of conversion falls to be considered.

Where a person was entitled to affirmative action under Article 16(4) of the

Constitution by reason of the social backwardness within the Hindu social

order, such entitlement is founded upon the disabilities which arose within,

and were produced by, that social structure. Upon conversion to Islam or

Christianity, or to any other non-Hindu social order in which caste is not

recognised as the basis of social status and classification, that foundational

basis ceases to operate in the same manner. The fact that the consequences

of the earlier disability may continue in the form of educational deprivation,

occupational      disadvantage,     economic     hardship    or   other    material

circumstances cannot carry the antecedent social backwardness into the new

religion. To permit such continuation would be to detach the consequences

from the social structure which produced them and to transpose social

backwardness of one religion into another religion in which such

backwardness is not recognised as the basis of social classification. The

constitutional benefit cannot be made to travel in this manner from the

religion in which the relevant backwardness arose to a religion whose basic

theological structure or otherwise does not recognise caste as its foundational

basis.


40.      The constitutional treatment of caste-based disadvantage furnishes

further indication of the same principle. Paragraph 3 of the Constitution

(Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950, as originally made under Article 341 of the

Constitution, restricted the Scheduled Caste status to persons professing the

Hindu religion, the subsequent constitutional amendments extended the



SLP (C) No.25507/2026                                                  Page 19 of 40
position to Sikhs and Buddhists, while persons professing Islam or

Christianity remain outside its scope. The provision operates specifically in

the field of Scheduled Caste status and cannot, by itself, determine every

question arising under Article 16(4) of the Constitution. It nevertheless

reflects the constitutional understanding that the status attached to caste-

based disability is not wholly detached from the social and religious order

within which that disability is constitutionally recognised. But a caste identity

cannot be treated as an immutable personal attribute carrying with it,

irrespective of a change in religious affiliation, every constitutional protection

or benefit which was available on account of that identity and the social

backwardness attaching to it.


41.   Consequently, where a person was receiving affirmative action under

Article 16(4) of the Constitution in the Hindu social order, upon conversion to

Islam, Christianity or to any other non-Hindu social order brings such

entitlement norms to an end.


B.    VALIDITY OF G.O. DATED 09.03.2024

42.   The distinction between religion and community assumes particular

significance in the present case. The fact that a person professes Islam does

not, by that circumstance alone, identify the particular Muslim community to

which he belongs. Muslim social organisation in India has historically

comprised a number of distinct groups, whose identities have, in different

regions and contexts, been associated with descent, occupation, locality,

ethnicity, customary affiliation and patterns of social association. The

material placed before us also indicates that the communities with which the


SLP (C) No.25507/2026                                                Page 20 of 40
present controversy is concerned have had distinct social histories and

identities; the Labbai, Rowther and Marakkayar, for instance, have been

separately described in the literature on the social organisation of Tamil

Muslims, even though they fall within the statutory entry relating to Labbais

in the State's Backward Class list. The seven categories like Dekkani Muslims,

Dudekula, Labbais including Rowthar and Marakayar, Mapilla, Sheik, Syed

and Ansar are likewise not a single undifferentiated category of Muslims, but

specifically identified communities within the State's scheme of backward-

class classification. It is against this distinction between religious identity and

membership of a particular notified community that the impugned G.O. must

now be examined, for the question is not merely what follows from a person's

conversion to Islam, but whether such conversion can, in law, furnish the

basis for treating him as a member of a particular notified Backward Class

Muslim community and extending to him the reservation attached to that

class.


43.      The fundamental premise of G.O. dated 09.03.2024 is that a person

belonging, before conversion, to a Backward Class, Most Backward Class,

Denotified Community or Scheduled Caste, who thereafter embraces Islam,

may be treated as a Backward Class Muslim and may be issued a community

certificate under one of the seven Muslim communities notified by the State

for which the State has reserved 3.5% of seats and posts for Backward Class

Muslims under Tamil Nadu Act 33 of 2007.


44.      The distinction which lies at the heart of the matter is between

continuance of a disadvantage and acquisition of membership of a particular


SLP (C) No.25507/2026                                                 Page 21 of 40
backward class. The proposition does not follow that conversion by itself

makes that person a member of a particular Muslim community already

notified as a backward class. The impugned G.O. proceeds from precisely

such a conflation. Respondent no. 1 was not seeking merely recognition of the

fact that he had become a Muslim, rather a certificate was sought specifically

one certifying him as a Muslim Labbai. This distinction is material as the

certificate of conversion issued by the Sunnath Jamath, Kayathar, recorded

that respondent no. 1 had embraced Islam and changed his name, however it

did not itself establish that he was born into or had historically belonged to

the Muslim Labbai community. The record shows that his application for a

Muslim Labbai certificate was rejected on the ground that respondent no. 1

converted to a religion and not to a caste or community.


45.   Before the High Court, the State sought to answer this difficulty by

submitting that the seven communities are already notified as Backward

Class Muslims and that the G.O. merely preserves the reservation benefit

which the proselyte enjoyed before conversion. But this explanation does not

answer the anterior question as to what is the legal basis upon which a person

who was not a member of one of those Muslim communities before conversion

becomes a member of that community after conversion. The answer to this

cannot be found in the fact of conversion itself as conversion establishes

religious affiliation and it does not, establish membership of a particular

socio-historical community within that religion. To reflect on this distinction,

we feel it imperative to place reliance on the observations made by the High

Court in G. Michael vs. S. Venkateswaran, Additional Secretary to

Michael (supra) had held that a Hindu converting to Islam ceased to belong

to his original caste and became a Muslim, and that his position in Muslim

society was not determined by the caste to which he had belonged before

conversion. The relevant observation made by the High Court are reproduced

or her entitlement to a public benefit. Such a power, carrying consequences

in the sphere of public law, must flow from law and cannot be assumed by a

private religious body by virtue of its communal or religious authority. This is

clear from the State's own submission, as recorded by the High Court,

59.   Now, it is apposite for us to recap our analysis on distinctive

understanding of the Hindu society and Muslim society. The distinction,

according to us, is not between a Muslim society which is wholly free from

social stratification and one which possesses a caste system identical to that

found in Hindu society. Social formations among Indian Muslims, including

the historically described categories of Ashraf, Ajlaf and Arzal, and the

numerous biradaris and occupational groups associated with them,

demonstrate that descent, occupation, endogamy and social status have, in

particular   regions    and   communities,   operated   as   bases     of   social

differentiation. At the same time, these categories cannot be treated as three

homogeneous castes constituting a single, uniform or universally applicable

hierarchy throughout Muslim society in India. Their content, boundaries and

social significance have varied across regions and communities.


60.   The constitutional inquiry must, therefore, remain anchored in the

social reality of the particular class sought to be identified, rather than in

either religious doctrine or a presumed religious-wide hierarchy. The fact that

Islam does not prescribe a caste hierarchy religion based on birth does not,

by itself, negate the existence of historically evolved forms of social

disadvantage among particular Muslim communities; equally, the existence

of such formations cannot justify treating every Muslim, or even every such

formation, as belonging to one predetermined caste-like class. What is

constitutionally relevant is the demonstrable social and educational

backwardness of the particular group, established by relevant and objective

criteria. This preserves the necessary distinction between what a religion

contexts, have organised themselves. Therefore, the idea of the State in the

present case drawing parallels with caste-based stratification in Hindu system

to that in Muslims is against the ethos of the Constitution.

CONCLUSION

62.   We therefore affirm the central conclusion of the High Court, though

our reasoning proceeds on the constitutional foundations set out above. A

person who converts to Islam does not, by that act alone, become a member

of any one of the seven notified Backward Class Muslim communities in the

State. His former caste or community status cannot automatically be

transposed into the Muslim Backward Class category, nor can a private

religious body conclusively determine such statutory entitlement.


63.   Tested on that standard, we are of the view that the impugned G.O.

cannot be sustained and has rightly been quashed by the High Court. It

creates an artificial route by which a person moves from a pre-conversion

establishing the necessary social and legal link. Therefore, the declaration

I.   BACKGROUND



1.   We heard the learned counsel appearing for the applicants and Mr.

     Tushar Mehta, the learned Solicitor General appearing for the Union

     of India.

2.   In our previous order dated 14.08.2026, we had expressed concerns

     over certain serious lapses on the part of various social media

     intermediaries and platforms, particularly in complying with the

     directions that were issued in our judgment dated 23.09.2024 in Just

     Rights for Children Alliance & Anr. v. S. Harish & Ors. reported in

     2024 INSC 716.


3.   In Just Rights (supra) we had taken note of an alarming increase in

     child sexual exploitation and abuse material (“CSEAM”) that were

     being circulated on social media platforms.


4.   At that time, we had flagged how indirect links to such harmful

     material were being promoted and shared through social media

     algorithms to bypass the rigours of the special penal provisions

       designed for the protection of children within the cyberspace, namely

5.     In our judgment, more particularly at paragraph 109, we had this to

       say: -

                It explained how the sellers and distributors of child

II. FRAMEWORK FOR THE DETECTION AND REMOVAL OF

      CSEAM.



A. Advanced Mechanisms for the Detection and Removal of CSEAM

 i.   Some Problems in the Existing Mechanism.


19. As far as we understand, the current mechanism for the detection and

      removal of CSEAM relies heavily on individual instances of content

      being reported and subsequently removed. These reports originate

      either at the behest of the authorities or the users themselves.



20. Although, various social media intermediaries have deployed their

      own safeguards for a seamless continued detection and removal of

      such content, yet what is missing is any form of synergy insofar as

      detection and removal is concerned, across the internet.


      M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                              Page 8 of 136
21. When one social media platform detects and removes CSEAM, that

      detection does not automatically result in the same content being

      flagged and removed from all other social media platforms.


22. It is only when such content is also found by the other platforms,

      through their own mechanisms and safeguards that, the same comes

      to be removed.


23. This isolated mechanism of detection delays the removal of CSEAM

      across different platforms, delays which enable the continued

      circulation of such content to the various corners of the internet.


24. Even if some social media platforms are coordinating their efforts for

      the simultaneous removal of CSEAM once so detected by either of one

      of them, such arrangements are only informal, dependent entirely on

      which platforms choose to undertake such initiative and for how long.



ii.   Matching and Listing of Hash & URL of CSEAM.


25. From what we have been able to understand, the practice that is

      globally in vogue for the seamless detection and removal of CSEAM

      is a process termed as “Hash and URL Data Matching & Listing”.


      M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                              Page 9 of 136
26. The process works on a simple principle. Every component of a

    CSEAM content, be it the video frame or image or multiples of both,

    carries a unique digital data print identifier in alphanumeric form,

    which is known as the “Hash” identifier of that material. The hash

    identifier of any particular content remains unique to it, irrespective

    of where it is uploaded or by whom.


27. When any content is identified as CSEAM, specialised software is

    used to extract and generate the hash identifier and the same is added

    to a consolidated database known as a “Hash List”.


28. This Hash List can then be used to crosscheck all other content,

    whether on the very same platform or on another. Where a match is

    found against a particular hash identifier, the algorithm automatically

    flags and removes that content without the need to rely on the

    conventional means of detection.


29. However, the above mechanism is not without limitations. Expert

    insights indicate that a new modus operandi has emerged for

    circumventing the hash list detection process. This is usually done by

    manipulating the video frame or imagery of the content, or a

    M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                             Page 10 of 136
    combination of both, either by way of resizing it or reformatting it, so

    as to avoid detection.


30. It is for this reason that “Perceptual Hashing”, an improved process of

    recent vintage assumes significance. Shorn of the details, this process,

    from what we understand, combines the original technique of

    extracting the hash identifier with an additional step of generating the

    audio-visual characteristics of the content. Characteristics such as

    colour-coding, object composition, audio cues, etc., are also used to

    generate the hash identifier for a content detected as CSEAM, which

    remains unique dehors any manipulation.


31. One another technological measure of similar significance that has

    caught our attention is URL Listing, which targets indirect links to

    CSEAM and other harmful content that are merely shared or

    exchanged on social media platforms without uploading or storing the

    same on the platform.


32. The news report that has been placed before us by the applicant herein

    reveals the prevalence of this very practice. It highlighted the

    circulation and promotion of CSEAM through links which would then




    M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                             Page 11 of 136
    redirect users to other websites and platforms where such materials

    were offered for monetary considerations.


33. “URL Listing” thus, assumes significance. Unlike Hash Listing that

    generates a unique identifier for the CSEAM content, URL Listing

    proceeds by generating an identifier for the external location where

    the CSEAM content is hosted. It extracts all possible unique web-

    addresses where the CSEAM has been confirmed to have been

    uploaded, and then uses that data to block any future attempts to

    access it.



34. Various jurisdictions across the world have, in some form or manner,

    called for the deployment of one, or a combination of the aforesaid

    measures, with a view to ensure the effective detection and removal

    of CSEAM.

37. These rules which came to be inserted by the Information Technology

    Amendment Rules, 2026, although a step in the right direction, yet,

    fall short as they do not speak of the specific tools and measures a

    social media intermediary must adopt.




    M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                                    Page 16 of 136
38. Rule 3(1) sub-clause (b), inter-alia, requires that intermediaries make

    reasonable efforts to ensure that their users do not host, upload or

    disseminate any CSEAM and other non-consensual sexually

    exploitative and abuse material, including those generated artificially,

    and to further remove such material under sub-clause (c).



39. Whereas Rule 4(4), inter-alia, requires a “significant social media

    intermediary” to also deploy “appropriate technical measures” for the

    detection and removal of CSEAM, including materials which are

    identical in content to any material that was previously flagged and

    deleted “on the computer resource of such intermediary”.


40. We would be remiss not to point out that the expression “on the

    computer resource of such intermediary” used in Rule 4 sub-rule (4)

    admits of certain ambiguities which need to be addressed.


41. In our considered view, the said expression narrowly confines the

    extent to which the technical measures must be deployed for the

    detection and removal of CSEAM.


42. The emphasis placed by Rule 4(4) on only that CSEAM content, which

    has been either detected or previously removed from the


    M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                                Page 17 of 136
    intermediary’s own computer resource, leaves unresolved two

    possible scenarios. First, the possibility of simultaneous flagging and

    removal of CSEAM content that was already removed on some other

    platform. Secondly, CSEAM content that is hosted on an external

    source and merely circulated on a particular platform via indirect

    links.


43. To state plainly, under this rule, even if a particular CSEAM was

    previously detected and removed by one intermediary, there is no

    corresponding     obligation   cast   upon   other   intermediaries    to

    automatically look for and remove the same, at least not until, such

    material happens to also be detected by them in due course of time.


44. This, in our view, confines the entire obligation of detection and

    removal of CSEAM exclusively to material that has been uploaded,

    circulated and detected on one intermediary’s own resources.


45. We, prima facie, find this to be a matter of some concern, particularly

    when there are reported instances of CSEAM being indirectly

    circulated, and a less than ideal rate at which such material is currently

    being detected and removed. It is needless to reiterate that every




    M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                               Page 18 of 136
    moment of delay in removing such harmful content only serves to add

    to the certain likelihood of further circulation to other platforms.



46. Even otherwise, the cumulative effect of the above rules is that social

    media intermediaries are only required to “make reasonable efforts” and

    “deploy appropriate technical measures” for the proactive detection and

    removal of CSEAM and other non-consensual sexually exploitative

    and abusive material from their platforms.


47. We are conscious of the fact that, at the current pace of advancement

    in technology, it is impractical to statutorily prescribe any particular

    set of tools and measures for a thriving, safe, and secure cyberspace.

51. We must, however, point out that the deployment of these tools

      cannot be the end of the matter. Unless the hashes and URLs of

      CSEAM identified by one intermediary are made accessible to all

      others, the very process of simultaneous flagging and removal of such

      material across platforms would remain illusory.



52. It is in this context that a national “Hash and URL List Database”

      assumes significance. As the name suggests, it is a common repository

      or pool of the hash identifiers and URL lists of all material which has

      been flagged and confirmed to be CSEAM across all platforms. The

      database is continuously updated in real time, and made accessible to

      all intermediaries and law enforcement agencies, to enable a seamless

      process of detection and removal of CSEAM on a rolling basis.


53. The significance of such a database may best be appreciated by

      contrasting it with the current state of affairs. At present, each

      intermediary, at best, maintains its own list of known CSEAM,

      compiled from what it has encountered on its own platform. The

    multiplicity in efforts in the detection and removal of CSEAM that we

    seek to avoid cannot take place without such a database.

    the content on their own platforms against the entire database, and

    not merely against what they themselves have encountered in the

    be recognised.

      developed and put in place a dedicated platform known as the

      “Sahyog Portal” to inter-alia streamline and automate the process of

      reporting and removal of unlawful content including CSEAM.



57. The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the authority

      designated to manage and maintain the portal, has been onboarding

      social media intermediaries onto the same, with a view to coordinate

      the reporting and removal of CSEAM with the police machinery.


58. We acknowledge that the Sahyog Portal is, no doubt, a step in the right

      direction. It is also not lost on us that the portal, by virtue of having

    reports and takedown notices.

61. We say so because there is a discernible difference between a common

    portal that routes individual reports and takedown notices, and one

    which pools together the hash identifiers and URLs of all material

    confirmed to be CSEAM. The former acts only upon each instance of

    such material, once identified, is continuously detected and removed

    across all platforms, without waiting for it to be reported afresh.

iii. Safeguards and Standard Operating Procedure for the Maintenance and
    Use of Hash & URL List Database.



63. The creation of a Hash & URL List Database of the kind indicated

    above naturally gives rise to certain attendant concerns, particularly

    the operation and procedural integrity of the same.



64. If the experiences of existing databases in other jurisdictions is any

    lodestar, the process by which a particular material comes to be

    entered into the database as CSEAM, and thereby earmarked for

    detection and removal, is perhaps the most sensitive of all.


65. From what we have been able to understand, the process by which a

    hash identifier or URL finds its way into any such database generally

    unfolds in three distinct stages: -



    M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                              Page 25 of 136
(i)    The first step of the process begins with the source of the

       material. The material which is ultimately entered into the

       database may come from a variety of sources. It may be reported

       by a member of the public, flagged by an intermediary on its

       own platform, forwarded by a law enforcement agency, or

       discovered by the body maintaining the database in the course

       of its own proactive search. It is of note, however, that the source

       of the material, by itself, is of little consequence, except in cases

       of hash matching, which we shall discuss in the later parts.

       Irrespective of where it originates, no material is to be

       mechanically entered into the database merely because it has

       been reported or flagged as CSEAM.

(ii)   The second, and perhaps the most crucial stage, is that of

       assessment, through multiple tiers of verification. This begins

       with a preliminary screening of the material by specialised

       software, which makes an initial determination, based on certain

       characteristics of the material, as to whether it is likely to be

       CSEAM. The software, however, does not have the final word.

       At the second tier, the material so flagged is assessed by at least

       three trained human analysts, who would independently



M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                                 Page 26 of 136
          determine whether the same constitutes CSEAM. This

          combination of software and human verification minimises

          erroneous inclusions and ensures that the database remains

          reliable to act upon.

    (iii) It is only upon such material being confirmed to be CSEAM that

          the third stage commences, wherein the hash identifier and/or

          the URL of the material is generated and entered into the

          database. This entry is then made available to all intermediaries

          and law enforcement agencies to cross-check against and

          remove any content matching the same.


66. The above process is to be carried out on a continuous basis, and the

    database updated at regular intervals. The entries within the database

    are to be made through encrypted channels and strictly confined to

    the hash identifier and/or URL of the material confirmed to be

    CSEAM. At no point should the CSEAM itself be stored within the

    database.

67. Since the above exercise for the detection and removal of CSEAM

    through means of ‘Hash Matching’ would be over and above the

    existing ordinary process of detection and removal, namely by way of

    due diligence and receipt of reports, certain additional aspects emerge

    that require clarification.



68. While the object of the above two parallel processes remains the same,

    that being the removal of CSEAM, yet there are certain differences

    between the two, which must be reflected in the standard operating

    procedure that would eventually come to be.


69. For this, we propose to draw a distinction between removal of CSEAM

    of “Unknown Origin” and “Known Origin”.


70. CSEAM of “Unknown Origin” would be all such material that has no

    corresponding match in the Hash & URL List Database but

    nevertheless was detected and subsequently removed on the basis of

    the intermediary’s own tools and mechanisms. In other words, that

    harmful material, which was found to be CSEAM on the basis of either

    reports received or as a result of the intermediary’s own due diligence.

71. Conversely, CSEAM of “Known Origin” would include all such

    material that is removed by an intermediary pursuant to a match

    significant difference in the procedure that an intermediary would be

73. Where an intermediary removes CSEAM of “Unknown Origin”, it

75. In addition, the intermediary would also be obligated to promptly

    report the same to the proper authorities under the relevant law, and

    also to the designated body for the Hash & URL List Database, if not

    Database.


93. Apart from the above, certain additional safeguards are also required

    to be put in place for the proper operation of such a database.


94. This is because an erroneous entry into the database would not only

    result in the removal of lawful content from one platform alone, but

    from every platform connected to the database.


95. This assumes all the more significance in the case of CSEAM of Known

    Origin, where the removal is triggered solely on the basis of a prior

    entry into the database. The removal follows automatically the

    M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                             Page 34 of 136
    moment a match is found, with no occasion for the intermediary to

    await any independent determination apropos the material.


96. Thus, it goes without saying that the use of Hash & URL List Database

    indicated above must be accompanied by adequate safeguards, some

    of which we may indicate, with the actual modalities left to be worked

    out by the Union of India. They are: -

    (i)    First, each entry into the database must be preceded by multiple

           tiers of independent verification of the material. The preliminary

           screening may be through specialised software, but the final

           assessment must mandatorily be made by two or three trained

           human analysts, each of whom would independently determine

           whether the same constitutes CSEAM.

    (ii)   Secondly, for each entry, the authority managing the database

           must maintain a report of the findings recorded in the course of

           its assessment. Such report must also bear the digital signatures

           of the analysts concerned, to ensure accountability for every

           inclusion.

    (iii) Thirdly, a complete record must also be kept by such authority

           of every entry in the database, the source from which the

           material originated, the analysts who assessed the same, their

    M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                              Page 35 of 136
       findings, and the date of its entry. Likewise, each and every

       access to the database, whether by an intermediary or an agency,

       must be logged. Such records must be preserved in a manner

       that permits the entries to be audited, and any lapse to be traced

       to its source.

(iv)   Fourthly, the Hash & URL List Database, and the entries made

       therein, must be subjected to periodic independent audits, the

       findings of which ought to be placed in the public domain, at

       least in an aggregated form.

(v)    Fifthly, where it is found that a particular hash identifier or URL

       came to be wrongly entered into the database, the same must be

       promptly removed therefrom. Such removal must also be

       communicated to all intermediaries, so that the content removed

       in consequence of such wrong entry is restored with immediate

       effect.

       by which any person aggrieved by the removal of content may

       raise a complaint, not merely with the intermediary, but also

 i.     Need to rethink and move beyond Section 79 of the IT Act.


223. If there is one theme that can be discerned from all our discussions

      above, it is the persistent failure of intermediaries, in one form or

      another, to comply with the various requirements envisaged under

      the IT Rules.



224. One reason that may explain why the intermediaries, despite being

      given numerous opportunities, continue to flout the IT Rules is the

      absence of any meaningful consequence for failing to comply with the

      IT Act and the rules thereunder.


225. Under the IT Act and rules framed thereunder, an intermediary which

      fails to observe or comply with any of its regulatory requirements,

      faces only one consequence; the loss of the “safe harbour” protection

      afforded to it under Section 79.


226. Once such protection is lost, the intermediary along with any person

      responsible for such failure, as the case may be, becomes liable for any

      content or information hosted on its platform, and may be prosecuted


      M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                             Page 83 of 136
    and punished for the same, under the relevant law for the time being

    in force. In the case of CSEAM, this would include offences under

    Section 15 and 67B of the POCSO and IT Act, respectively.


227. The consequence of an intermediary’s failure to comply with the

    requirements of the law in discharge of its duty is confined to it being

    held liable for and proceeded against, qua a particular content or

    information, which constitutes an offence under any law for the time

    being in force.


228. In other words, it fastens a post facto liability upon the defaulting

    intermediary, only after an offence is committed, by the upload,

    publication or hosting of any particular content or information on its

    platform.


229. Although such an approach may be suitable where the harm sought

    to be addressed is capable of being remedies after the fact, yet the same

    cannot be said for CSEAM.


230. The harm that is occasioned by such material is not confined to the

    moment of its creation. Every instance of its circulation, every view,

    and every download, revictimizes the child depicted therein.



    M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                              Page 84 of 136
231. The continued circulation of CSEAM does irreparable harm to the

    society. It fuels the consumption and demand for such exploitative

    and abusive material; it normalises abuse of children and emboldens

    those who seek it out.


232. In such a scenario, the post facto prosecution and punishment,

    howsoever successful, of those responsible for allowing the upload,

    circulation and viewing of CSEAM, even if indirectly or inadvertently,

    can hardly undo the harm that has already been done.



233. Even otherwise, Section 79 of the IT Act does not address the systemic

    lapses and their continuance the on part of the intermediaries in

    discharge of their duties in accordance with the law. Despite the

    requirement to observe due diligence in their functioning, the said

    provision springs into action not upon a wilful failure to do the same,

    but only after the commission of any offence in consequence thereof.



234. In other words, it does not address the failure to comply, but only the

    aftermath that follows such failure. An intermediary may persistently

    fail to comply with the requirements of the IT Act and the rules



    M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026                              Page 85 of 136
    thereunder, and yet face no consequence whatsoever, unless and until
